Kartli and Kakheti. Georgian has been written since the 5th century.
Georgian spread west as the language of church and kingdom.
The Abasgoi and Apsilai of Greek writers.
The languages of Caucasian Albania. One was written from the 5th century and survives as Udi.
Lezgian and its relatives in the north of Azerbaijan.
Persian speakers settled in Shirvan and around Baku under the Sasanians. Tat is a small language today.
Oghuz Turkic arrived with the Seljuks in the 11th century and was the main language by about 1500.
Adyghe and Kabardian, from the Black Sea coast to the Kuban.
Adygea. Most Circassians were driven out to the Ottoman Empire in 1864.
Kabardian.
Sarmatian and then Alan speech on the plains north of the mountains.
Ossetian, the descendant of Alan, in the central valleys.
Chechen, Ingush, Avar, Dargwa, Lak, Lezgian and some thirty more languages. Their long presence is inferred from the depth of the family.
Kipchak Turkic on the steppe north of the mountains after the Mongol conquest: Nogai, Kumyk and Karachay-Balkar.
Nogai and Kumyk today. Karachay and Balkar are spoken in the high valleys to the west.
Cossack and Russian settlement along the Kuban and the Terek, from the late 18th century.
Settled from Norway and the Norse settlements in Britain and Ireland from about 870. The island had no people before, apart perhaps from a few Irish hermits.
The speech of the villages of Syria and Palestine. Greek was the language of the cities and of government.
Aramaic in Mesopotamia, in the dialects of the Babylonian Talmud, the Mandaeans and the Church of the East.
Edessa, Nisibis and Tur Abdin, the home of Syriac.
Arabic replaced Aramaic between about 700 and 1100, last in the north and in the mountains.
Mount Lebanon and the Qalamun, where Aramaic lasted longest in Syria. Three villages near Maaloula still speak it.
Neo-Aramaic of the Christians and Jews of Tur Abdin, Hakkari and the Mosul plain.
The Mosul plain and the valleys north of it. Many speakers have left Iraq since 2003.
Hebrew was still spoken in Judaea beside Aramaic. It went out of daily use after the revolt of 132 to 135.
Hebrew was revived as an everyday language by Jewish settlers from the 1880s.
Israel. Arabic is spoken beside it.
The Negev.
Phoenician on the coast of Tyre and Sidon, giving way to Aramaic and Greek.
Punic, the Phoenician of Carthage, in Tunisia and eastern Algeria. Augustine heard it in the countryside about 400.
Tripolitania, where Punic was written in Latin letters into the 4th century.
Arabic and the closely related Old North Arabian dialects of the Hejaz and Najd, known before Islam from thousands of rock inscriptions.
Nabataea and the Negev. The Nabataeans wrote Aramaic and spoke Arabic.
Nomads of the Syrian desert, who left the Safaitic inscriptions in the first centuries CE. Thinly peopled.
The Gulf coast and its hinterland. Thinly peopled away from the coast.
The Empty Quarter, crossed by a few nomads and otherwise without people.
Oman, where Arab tradition brings the Azd in the first centuries CE. What was spoken before is not known.
Arabic replaced the Old South Arabian languages of Yemen about 600.
Hadramawt.
Arabic spread from the garrison towns and the desert edge after the conquest of the 630s and was the common speech by about 1000.
Iraq, from the garrison towns of Kufa and Basra.
Jordan and the Negev.
Sabaic, Minaic and Qatabanic in the highlands of Yemen, written until the 6th century.
Hadramitic in the Hadramawt.
The Modern South Arabian languages, a separate branch from the written languages of Yemen. Their early extent is inferred, and the land was thinly peopled.
Mehri, Jibbali and their relatives in Mahra and Dhofar.
Soqotra.
Egyptian, written in Demotic and from the 3rd century in the Coptic alphabet.
The oases of the western desert. Empty of people between them.
Arabic replaced Coptic between about 700 and 1300, first in the Delta and the towns.
Upper Egypt, where Coptic was spoken longest. Reports of later speakers are doubtful.
Alexandria, the largest Greek-speaking city of its time.
Cyrene and its four sister cities, Greek since the 7th century BCE.
Nomads of the eastern desert, the Blemmyes of ancient writers, taken to have spoken an early form of Beja. Thinly peopled.
The Bisharin Beja of the far south-east. The Ababda north of them now speak Arabic.
Lower Nubia, south of Aswan, where Meroitic was written until the 4th century and Nubian after it. The desert on either side is empty.
Most Egyptian Nubians were moved north to Kom Ombo when the Aswan High Dam flooded their valley in 1964.
Arab nomads of Sinai and the desert east of the Delta. Thinly peopled.
Fustat, the Delta and the towns, after the conquest of 641.
The language of nearly all Egyptians since about 1300. The deserts are thinly peopled.
Bedouin of the coast west of Alexandria.
Berber, called Tamazight by its speakers, in Morocco.
Algeria and Tunisia. The Libyan inscriptions of Numidia are in an early form of the language.
Tripolitania and the Fezzan.
Cyrenaica and the Libyan desert. Thinly peopled.
The oases west of the Nile. Thinly peopled.
Siwa, the one Berber-speaking oasis of Egypt.
The western Sahara, home of the Sanhaja nomads. Thinly peopled.
The sand seas between the Draa and the Niger bend. Almost empty.
The central Sahara, where Tuareg speak Tamasheq. Very thinly peopled.
The Rif, the Atlas and the Sous, where Berber held while Arabic took the plains.
Kabylia and the Aures.
The Nafusa hills, Zuwara, Ghadames and the island of Djerba.
The languages of the Canary Islands, known from words and names and taken to be Berber. The date of first settlement is disputed.
Fuerteventura and Lanzarote.
Castile conquered the islands between 1402 and 1496.
The eastern islands were taken first.
Latin in the towns and farms of Africa Proconsularis and Numidia.
The coast of Mauretania.
A Romance speech lasted in a few towns of Tunisia. Arab geographers still mention it in the 12th century.
Kairouan, Tunis and the towns of Ifriqiya.
Fez and the towns of the north.
Bedouin Arabic spread over the plains after the Banu Hilal arrived about 1050.
The plains and plateaus of Algeria.
Tripolitania and Cyrenaica, settled by the Banu Sulaym.
The Libyan desert. Very thinly peopled.
The Atlantic plains of Morocco, settled by Arab nomads under the Almohads.
The oases and nomads of the northern Sahara. Thinly peopled.
Hassaniya Arabic, brought by the Banu Hassan and taken up by the Sanhaja. Thinly peopled.
The sand seas south of the Draa, crossed by Arabic-speaking nomads. Almost empty.
The Teda or Tubu of the southern Libyan desert, on the edge of Tibesti. Very thinly peopled, and their early history is not recorded.
Celts who crossed into Anatolia in 278 BCE. Their land became a Roman province in 25 BCE.
A client kingdom until Rome annexed it in 17. A Cappadocian language is reported into the 4th century.
Phrygian was still cut on gravestones in the 2nd and 3rd centuries.
Mountain people of the Taurus who raided the lowlands. One of them became the emperor Zeno in 474.
The remainder of the kingdom of Mithridates, ruled by the house of Polemon and annexed by Rome in 64.
A small kingdom on the Euphrates whose kings claimed Greek and Persian descent. Rome annexed it in 72.
The Byzantine state in exile after 1204. It retook Constantinople in 1261.
A Greek state on the Pontic coast under the Komnenos family, taken by the Ottomans in 1461.
The Seljuk sultanate of Anatolia, with its capital at Konya. Rum means Rome.
Tributary to the Mongols after the battle of Kose Dag in 1243.
Turkmen rulers of Sivas and Malatya, absorbed by the sultans of Rum.
The strongest of the beyliks and the last to fall to the Ottomans.
Aydin, Menteshe, Saruhan and Germiyan. Ibn Battuta visited their courts in the 1330s.
The White Sheep Turkmen of Diyarbakir. After 1467 they ruled Iran as well, until the Safavids.
The Black Sheep Turkmen of Lake Van and Azerbaijan, who also held Baghdad.
The Turkish-speaking Muslims of Anatolia, the core of the Ottoman Empire and of the republic.
Arab writers name Kurds in the mountains north and east of Mosul from the time of the conquests.
Divided since the 1920s between Turkey, Iraq, Syria and Iran. The Kurdistan Region of Iraq has governed itself since 1991.
A Kurdish dynasty at Mayyafariqin and Amid, now Diyarbakir.
A Kurdish dynasty at Ganja and Dvin. A branch held Ani until 1199.
Bitlis, Bohtan, Hakkari, Soran, Baban and others, hereditary emirs between the Ottomans and Persia. The Ottomans removed the last about 1850.
A Kurdish-speaking religious community of Sinjar and Sheikhan, formed around the tomb of Sheikh Adi, who died in 1162. Many were killed or driven out in 2014.
Contested between Rome and Parthia and ruled by a branch of the Parthian royal house from the 50s. It was Christian from the early 4th century, and the kingship ended in 428.
Governed by Persian marzbans while the nobles kept their lands. The alphabet was made about 405 and the revolt of 451 fills the chronicles.
The restored kingdom, with its capital at Ani. Byzantium annexed it in 1045.
The Artsruni kingdom around Lake Van.
A principality of Armenian settlers from about 1080 and a kingdom from 1198. The Mamluks took its capital Sis in 1375.
Without a state, under Ottoman and Persian and from 1828 Russian rule. Most Armenians of Anatolia were deported and killed in 1915.
A republic in 1918, a Soviet republic from 1920 and independent since 1991.
The east Georgian kingdom, with its capital at Mtskheta, Christian from about 330. Persia ended the kingship about 580.
Ruled by princes under Persian, Byzantine and then Arab overlords. Tbilisi was an Arab emirate from the 8th century.
Ancient Colchis, a client of Rome. Rome and Persia fought for it from 541 to 562.
Founded by Abkhaz princes, it covered western Georgia and used Georgian in church and court.
The Bagrationi principality in the south-west, from which the kings of united Georgia came.
United in 1008 and at its height under David IV and Tamar, about 1200. Mongols and Timur broke it and it divided by about 1490.
The eastern kingdoms, under Safavid Persia for most of the period. Russia annexed them in 1801.
The western kingdom, under Ottoman influence. Russia annexed it in 1810.
A kingdom between the Kura and the Caspian, unrelated to Albania in the Balkans. Strabo says its people spoke many languages.
Iranian-speaking horsemen north of the Caucasus passes.
The kingdom of Alania, Christian from the early 10th century. The Mongols destroyed it in 1238 and 1239.
Descendants of the Alans in the central valleys. South Ossetia broke from Georgia in the 1990s and its status is disputed.
They call themselves Adyghe, and Greek writers call them Zichoi. Russia conquered them in 1864 and most were driven out.
Those who stayed, in Adygea and nearby.
The Abasgoi, with princes of their own under Roman influence.
Abkhazia broke from Georgia in 1993 and its status is disputed.
The mountain kingdom Arab geographers call Sarir, the Throne.
The Avar khanate at Khunzakh. Unrelated to the Avars of the Danube.
Called Durdzuks in the Georgian chronicles.
Deported to Central Asia in 1944 and allowed back in 1957.
The state of the imams of Dagestan and Chechnya. Shamil led its war against Russia until 1859.
The Shirvanshahs, an Arab house that became Persian in speech and ruled until the Safavids took their land in 1538.
Karabakh, Ganja, Shirvan, Baku, Erivan and others, under Persian suzerainty until Russia took them between 1804 and 1828.
Turkic-speaking Shia Muslims north of the Aras. More Azerbaijanis live south of it, in Iran.
The kingdom of the Abgars at Edessa, where Syriac became a written language. Rome ended it about 242.
A kingdom around Arbela under Parthian overlords. Josephus tells how its royal house became Jewish about 30.
A desert city whose rulers wrote Aramaic and called themselves kings of the Arabs. The Sasanians destroyed it in 241.
A trading kingdom at the head of the Gulf, also called Mesene, under Parthian overlords.
A caravan city of Aramaic and Arab families inside the Roman province of Syria.
Under Odaenathus and Zenobia it held Syria, Egypt and part of Anatolia, until Aurelian took the city.
The Church of the East and the Syriac Orthodox, in Tur Abdin, Hakkari and the Mosul plain.
Driven from Hakkari and Tur Abdin in 1915. Many have left Iraq since 2003.
A baptising community of the southern marshes with its own Aramaic scriptures. Most have left Iraq since 2003.
The kingdom of the Herods and then a Roman province. The revolts of 66 to 73 and 132 to 135 destroyed Jerusalem and emptied much of Judaea.
After 135 the centre of Jewish life in Palestine was Galilee, where the Mishnah and the Jerusalem Talmud were compiled. They spoke Aramaic and wrote Hebrew.
Around Mount Gerizim. Their revolts of 484 and 529 were put down, and a few hundred Samaritans remain today.
A large community under its own exilarch. The academies of Sura and Pumbedita compiled the Babylonian Talmud by about 500.
The Phoenician cities under Rome. Phoenician was still written on their coins in the 1st century.
Jewish settlers in Ottoman and then British Palestine, who made Hebrew a spoken language again.
Hebrew speakers of the state founded in 1948. A fifth of its citizens are Arabs.
The Negev.
The people of the Nile valley under Roman and Byzantine governors. Papyri record their villages in more detail than any other people of the time.
Egyptian Christians under Muslim rule, a majority until about the 10th century. The Coptic church continues, with Arabic-speaking members.
A Greek city with a large Jewish community until the revolt of 115 to 117.
Desert nomads who raided Upper Egypt from the 3rd century. They are usually taken to be ancestors of the Beja.
Arab geographers describe the Beja and the gold mines of their desert. Most Beja live further south, in Sudan.
Christians of Mount Lebanon, in union with Rome since the Crusades. They spoke Aramaic at first and keep Syriac in church.
A community that grew from Fatimid Ismaili teaching about 1017, in the Shuf and on Mount Hermon.
Jabal al-Druze, settled from Lebanon in the 18th century.
The coastal mountains of Syria. Older writers call them Nusayris.
The castles around Masyaf, held by the sect the Crusaders called the Assassins until Baybars took them.
The Arab kingdom of Petra and Hegra, which wrote in Aramaic. Trajan made it the province of Arabia in 106.
A people of the northern Hejaz named by Pliny and Ptolemy and in a temple inscription of the 160s.
The oldest of the South Arabian kingdoms, with its capital at Marib. Himyar absorbed it about 275.
A highland kingdom with its capital at Zafar, named in the Periplus.
Himyar united South Arabia by about 300. Its kings turned to Judaism about 380, and Aksum conquered it in 525.
Under Aksumite viceroys, among them Abraha, and from the 570s under Persian governors.
The frankincense kingdom, with its capital at Shabwa. Himyar conquered it about 300.
At Qaryat al-Faw, on the road from Yemen to the Gulf.
Kings of Kinda ruled the nomads of central Arabia on behalf of Himyar. The poet Imru al-Qays was of their house.
Arab kings at al-Hira who guarded the desert frontier for the Sasanians. Khusraw II ended the dynasty in 602.
Christian Arab allies of Constantinople on the Syrian desert edge, from 529 under one chief.
The people of Mecca and of Muhammad. Their early history was written down two centuries later.
Arab tradition brings the Azd from Yemen to Oman. The Sasanians held the coast.
The first independent rulers of Muslim Egypt, founded by a Turkish governor of the Abbasids.
An Arab house at Mosul and Aleppo. Sayf al-Dawla fought Byzantium and kept the poet al-Mutanabbi.
An Ismaili state in eastern Arabia that carried off the Black Stone from Mecca in 930.
Emirs of Ifriqiya at Kairouan for the Abbasids. They conquered Sicily.
A descendant of Ali founded a state among the Berbers of northern Morocco and his son founded Fez.
Ismaili caliphs raised to power in Ifriqiya by the Kutama Berbers.
They took Egypt in 969 and founded Cairo. Saladin ended the caliphate in 1171.
Imams at Sada and Sanaa, ruling the northern highlands in most centuries. Their last kingdom ended in 1962.
Sultans of Taizz and Zabid, of Turkmen origin, who grew rich on the Aden trade.
The house of Saladin, Kurdish by origin. He took Jerusalem from the Crusaders in 1187.
Syria, divided among princes of the family until the Mongols came.
Descendants of the Prophet who governed the Hejaz under Egyptian and then Ottoman overlords. Ibn Saud took their kingdom in 1925.
Ibadi imams elected at Nizwa.
The Yaruba imams drove the Portuguese from Muscat in 1650. The Al Bu Said, from 1749, ruled Zanzibar as well.
Sharifs from the Draa who united Morocco and defeated Portugal in 1578 and Songhay in 1591.
Sharifs from Tafilalt, the ruling house of Morocco to this day.
The alliance of the house of Saud with the reformer Ibn Abd al-Wahhab. An Egyptian army destroyed Diriyah in 1818.
The second state, at Riyadh, lost to the Al Rashid of Hail in 1891.
The Al Rashid, chiefs of the Shammar, who ruled northern Najd until Ibn Saud took Hail.
Bedouin sent west from Egypt about 1050. Ibn Khaldun blamed them for the ruin of Ifriqiya, and their dialects made the plains Arabic-speaking.
They moved west with the Banu Hilal and settled Cyrenaica and Tripolitania.
Camel nomads who moved from Najd into the Syrian desert in the 18th century.
Nomads of Jabal Shammar. A branch crossed into the Jazira of Iraq in the 17th century.
Hassaniya-speaking nomads of Arab and Sanhaja descent. Sovereignty over Western Sahara is disputed between Morocco and the Polisario Front.
The Arabic-speaking people of Palestine, many of them refugees since 1948. The status of the West Bank and Gaza is disputed.
The Moors. Their kingdom of Mauretania, under Juba II and his son, was annexed by Rome in 40.
The kingdom ended in 46 BCE. Its people left inscriptions in the Libyan script.
Tacfarinas led them against Rome from 17 to 24.
A general Roman name for the herders of the steppe south of the provinces.
Farmers and traders of the Fezzan, who watered their oases by underground channels. Their capital was Garama.
Nomads of the Gulf of Sirte and the oasis of Augila.
Nomads of Tripolitania. Ammianus names Austuriani here in the 360s, who may be the same people, and Corippus describes the Laguatan wars of the 540s.
An inscription of 508 at Altava names Masuna, king of the Moors and the Romans.
Iaudas fought the Byzantines here in the 530s. Arab tradition makes the queen called the Kahina its last ruler, about 700.
Ibadi imams at Tahert, of Persian descent, chosen and followed by Berber peoples.
A Berber state on the Atlantic plain with a prophet and a scripture of its own, destroyed by the Almoravids.
The Midrarid emirs of the caravan city at the head of the gold road to the Sudan.
Sanhaja Berbers left to govern Ifriqiya when the Fatimids moved to Cairo.
A branch of the Zirids in the central Maghreb, first at the Qala and then at Bejaia.
Zenata Berbers who took Morocco from the Almohads and ruled from Fez.
Kinsmen of the Marinids, who held Fez while Portugal took the Atlantic ports.
Zenata Berbers at Tlemcen, pressed between Fez and Tunis.
Almohad governors of Masmuda descent who made Tunis their capital. They ruled in Arabic.
Mountain people of Lesser Kabylia, the army that brought the Fatimids to power.
One of Ibn Khaldun's three great Berber groupings, herders of the high plains.
Farmers of the High Atlas, among whom the Almohad movement began.
Veiled camel nomads of the western Sahara, among them the Lamtuna, who made the Almoravid empire.
They call themselves Kel Tamasheq. Ibn Battuta crossed the Ahaggar in 1353, and their confederations there and in the Ajjer held the Saharan roads.
Ibadi Berbers who founded the five towns of the Mzab in the 11th century.
The largest Berber-speaking people of Algeria, in the mountains east of Algiers.
Berbers of the Rif mountains. Their republic fought Spain and France from 1921 to 1926.
The Berbers of the High Atlas and the Sous, called Shilha or Chleuh by outsiders.
The first people of the Canary Islands, known from archaeology and from their conquerors. Castile took the last island, Tenerife, in 1496.
Slave soldiers, first Kipchak Turks and later Circassians, who ruled Egypt over an Arabic-speaking people.
Syria, held after the Mongols were beaten at Ayn Jalut in 1260. The Ottomans took it in 1516.
The first four caliphs, at Medina. Their armies took Syria, Iraq, Egypt and Persia between 634 and 651.
Ruled from Damascus. At its widest it reached from Spain to the Indus.
Baghdad was founded in 762. The provinces went their own way in the 9th century and the Buyids of Iran took Baghdad in 945.
Caliphs under Buyid and Seljuk guardians, ruling Iraq themselves again in the 12th century. The Mongols killed the last in 1258.
A Mongol house that kept Iraq after the Ilkhanate of Persia broke up.
Founded by the First Crusade. French-speaking lords ruled Arabic-speaking Muslims and Christians.
After Saladin took Jerusalem the kingdom was a strip of coast governed from Acre, which fell in 1291.
The first Crusader state and the first to fall.
A Norman principality, taken by the Mamluk sultan Baybars in 1268.
The Lusignan kings ruled a Greek-speaking island. Venice held it from 1489 and the Ottomans took it in 1571.
An Ottoman province founded by the Barbarossa brothers and ruled in practice by its own deys.
Ottoman from 1574 and ruled by the Husainid beys from 1705.
Ottoman from 1551, under the Karamanli family from 1711 to 1835.
France took Algiers in 1830 and settled the coast. Independence came in 1962 after eight years of war.
Spain held a zone in the north and another in the far south.
Spain withdrew in 1975. Sovereignty over the territory has been disputed since.
Italy took the coast from the Ottomans in 1911 and the interior by 1931.
Under British administration by mandate of the League of Nations.
Britain took the port of Aden in 1839 and made treaties with the sultans inland.
Russia annexed eastern Georgia in 1801 and took the rest from Persia and the Ottomans by 1829 and 1878.
Georgia, Armenia and Azerbaijan were independent from 1918 to 1921 and then Soviet republics until 1991.
Muhammad Ali and his heirs ruled as Ottoman viceroys in name.
Under British occupation.
A kingdom from 1922 and a republic from 1953.
Ibn Saud took Riyadh in 1902 and the Hejaz in 1925, and named the kingdom in 1932.
North and South Yemen united in 1990. The country has been divided by war since 2014.
The sultanate of Muscat and Oman, called Oman since 1970.
Seven sheikhdoms, the Trucial States under British protection from the 19th century.
A sheikhdom of the Al Sabah from the 18th century, under British protection from 1899 to 1961.
A kingdom under British mandate from 1921, independent in 1932 and a republic from 1958.
The emirate of Transjordan from 1921 and a kingdom from 1946.
Founded in 1948. It has occupied the West Bank since 1967, and the status of the Palestinian territories is disputed.
The Palestinian Authority has administered parts of the West Bank and Gaza since 1994. Statehood and borders are disputed.
Independent from Britain in 1960 and divided since 1974. Only Turkey recognises the state declared in the north.
The status of Abkhazia and South Ossetia is disputed.
A kingdom from 1951 and a republic from 1969. Rival governments have divided it since 2014.
Morocco has held most of Western Sahara since 1975. Sovereignty over it is disputed.
Western Anatolia, Greek on the coast since before 1 CE and in the interior by about 500.
The cities and coasts of Pamphylia and Cilicia.
Greek replaced the old languages of the interior and was the speech of Byzantine Anatolia until the Turkish settlement.
Pontus, Greek-speaking until the exchange of populations in 1923.
Western Anatolia under the last Byzantine emperors.
Smyrna and the Aegean coast, until 1923.
Cappadocian Greek villages.
Cyprus.
Anatolia, the heart of the empire until the Seljuks won at Manzikert in 1071.
Syria, Palestine and Egypt, lost to the Arabs between 634 and 642.
Africa, retaken from the Vandals in 533 and 534 and held until the Arabs took Carthage in 698.
The west and the coasts of Anatolia, recovered behind the First Crusade.
The beylik of Osman in Bithynia. Bursa was its capital from 1326.
Western and central Anatolia, lost to Timur in 1402 and regained.
All Anatolia after the conquests of 1461 to 1517. The sultanate was abolished in 1922.
Syria from 1516 and Iraq from 1534, with a frontier against Safavid Persia fixed in 1639.
Egypt, governed through its Mamluk households.
The Hejaz and at times Yemen.
The eastern provinces: Anatolia, Syria, and Egypt. The frontier with Parthia and then Sasanian Persia ran along the Euphrates.
The African provinces, from Cyrenaica to Mauretania.
The republic founded in 1923, with its capital at Ankara.
The Vandal kingdom of Africa. Carthage fell to them in 439 and to Belisarius in 533.
A reform movement among the Sanhaja of the Sahara. They founded Marrakesh about 1062.
A movement of the Masmuda of the High Atlas, begun by Ibn Tumart. Marrakesh fell to the Marinids in 1269.
The central and eastern Maghreb as far as Tripoli.
Parthian was written at Nisa before 1 CE and later in Sasanian royal inscriptions. It gave way to Persian by about the 7th century.
The central deserts of Iran, thinly peopled.
Aria, the country around Herat. Its Iranian speech is not recorded and is shown with Parthian.
Media and Atropatene. Median is known only from names and loanwords.
Old Azari, the Iranian language of Azerbaijan that the Arab geographers mention. Turkic replaced it between the 11th and the 17th century, and Tati is its remnant.
Persis, under its own kings, who put Persian legends on their coins.
The language of the Sasanian state and of the Zoroastrian books. It spread over the whole plateau.
Carmania and Makran, thinly peopled. Which languages were spoken here is not recorded, and Persian is shown for want of evidence.
Merv, Herat and Sistan, the Sasanian east, where Persian began to replace Parthian and Bactrian.
New Persian, written in Arabic script from the 9th century.
Khurasan and what is now Afghanistan, where the language is called Dari. It includes the Hazaragi of the central mountains.
Transoxiana, where Persian replaced Sogdian under the Samanids. Here it is called Tajik.
The Merv oasis, Persian-speaking until Turkmen settled it.
The central Zagros. Arab writers name Kurds here from the 7th century, and Kurdish is first written in the 16th.
Kurds moved to northern Khurasan by Shah Abbas about 1600 to hold the frontier.
Close relatives of Persian in the southern Zagros.
Gilan. The early speech of the Caspian shore is inferred from its later languages.
Mazandaran, the old Tabaristan. The Caspian languages kept apart behind the Alborz, and Mazandarani was written from the 10th century.
Balochi is a north-western Iranian language. Its speakers moved into Makran from about 1000.
The Helmand deserts, thinly peopled.
Oghuz Turkic arrived with the Seljuks in the 11th century and was general in Azerbaijan by the 16th.
Turkic speakers around Zanjan, Qazvin and Hamadan.
Khuzestan. Arab settlement began with the conquest and grew from the 15th century.
Arabic-speaking ports of the Gulf coast.
Oghuz Turkic spread over the Karakum from the 11th century. Much of this land is desert and thinly peopled.
The Gorgan plain in Iran.
North-western Afghanistan.
The Qashqai of Fars, who moved each year between the Gulf lowlands and the Zagros.
Khorasani Turkic.
Written in Greek letters on Kushan coins and inscriptions and in legal documents down to the 8th century.
The central mountains of Afghanistan, thinly peopled. Their speech is not recorded.
Pashto descends from an eastern Iranian language of this region. It has no sure record before the 16th century, so the early area is a guess.
Pashtuns spread west to Kandahar and Herat from about 1500.
Pashtuns were settled in the north from the 1880s.
The Kabul valley spoke Indo-Aryan languages and was counted as part of India by Xuanzang.
Pashai and the Nuristani languages, which kept to the mountain valleys.
Shughni, Wakhi and their relatives, eastern Iranian languages of the high valleys. Thinly peopled.
The Zarafshan valley, with Samarkand and Bukhara. Yaghnobi, spoken in one valley of Tajikistan, descends from it.
Sogdian trading towns along the Chu and the Talas.
The lower Amu Darya. Al-Biruni, a native speaker, records its calendar, and glosses were still written in the 13th century.
Sakas settled in Drangiana about 100 BCE. It became Sakastan, now Sistan.
Dahae and other nomads of the Karakum. Thinly peopled.
The Aral Sea and the Syr Darya, home of the Massagetae of the Greeks and the Kangju of the Chinese. Their Iranian speech is inferred from names.
Fergana, the Tian Shan and the Ili. The Wusun lived here too and their language is not known.
The Kazakh steppe and the forest edge north of it. Iranian speech is inferred from burials of Saka and Sarmatian type, and the land was thinly peopled.
The Altai, where the frozen tombs of Saka type end shortly before this period.
Huns and other peoples crossed the steppe from the 4th century. What they spoke is not known, and Iranian and early Turkic were both still heard.
The Volga and the Don after the Huns crossed them about 370.
Turkic spread across the steppe with the khaganate of 552. Runiform inscriptions stand on the Talas.
Semirechye and the Tian Shan. Western Turks, Turgesh and Karluks, then the Turkic of the Kara-Khanids and of Moghulistan.
Turkic nomads east of the Caspian. Thinly peopled.
Turkic speakers of the upper Irtysh and the Altai foothills.
Khazar and Oghur Turkic on the lower Volga. Chuvash is the only living language of this branch.
The Oghuz lived between the Aral Sea and the Syr Darya before the Seljuks led many of them south.
Kimeks on the Irtysh and then Kipchaks gave the steppe its Persian name, Dasht-i Qipchaq.
Kipchak became the common speech of the Golden Horde.
Between the Don and the Volga, the Polovtsy of the Russian chronicles.
Kipchak speakers of the Aral shore and northern Khwarezm.
The western steppe, the land of the Junior Zhuz.
Kazakh took shape from the Kipchak of the eastern steppe after 1465. The land is thinly peopled.
Semirechye and the upper Irtysh.
Karluk Turkic settled among Persian speakers under the Kara-Khanids. Its literary form was Chagatai and it is now Uzbek.
The Fergana valley.
Khwarezm, where Turkic replaced Khwarezmian.
Northern Afghanistan, settled by Uzbeks from the 16th century.
Kyrgyz are recorded in the Tian Shan from about 1500. How they relate to the Kyrgyz of the Yenisei is debated.
The Amu Darya delta. The land around it is desert.
Dzungar pastures on the Irtysh and in Semirechye, lost when the Qing destroyed the Dzungars in the 1750s.
Kalmyks, Oirats who moved to the lower Volga about 1630. Most of those east of the river left for Dzungaria in 1771.
Kalmykia. The Kalmyks were deported in 1943 and allowed back in 1957.
Novgorod settlers reached the Dvina and the White Sea from the 12th century.
After the fall of Kazan in 1552 Russian settlement moved down the Volga.
The lower Volga, settled after Astrakhan fell in 1556.
The lower Don, where Cossack settlements appear in the 16th century.
The Urals, with mines and ironworks from about 1700.
The Orenburg line of forts, begun in the 1730s.
Tyumen was founded in 1586 and Tobolsk in 1587. Peasants followed the forts.
Tomsk was founded in 1604 and Krasnoyarsk in 1628. The farmland of the south filled in the 18th and 19th centuries.
Along the road and later the railway toward Irkutsk.
Northern Kazakhstan. Cossack lines in the 18th century, peasant settlers from the 1890s and the Virgin Lands campaign of the 1950s. Many left after 1991.
Verny, now Almaty, and the settlers of Semirechye.
Mining and gas towns of the north, such as Norilsk and Novy Urengoy. Outside them the land is very thinly peopled.
Mordvin, in two languages, Erzya and Moksha. Jordanes names the Mordens in the 6th century, and the earlier area is inferred.
Mari, the Cheremis of the Russian chronicles.
Merya, Muroma and Meshchera, who took up Russian. Their languages are unrecorded and their place in the family is uncertain.
Komi, in thinly peopled forest. It was first written by Stephen of Perm in the 1370s, and the earlier area is inferred.
Udmurt, between the Kama and the Vyatka.
The Chud beyond the portage of the Novgorod chronicles. Their language is assumed to be Finnic from place names.
The usual placing of the Hungarian homeland, on both sides of the southern Urals. It rests on the language and on archaeology and is disputed.
Those who stayed when the Magyars went west. The friar Julian found Hungarian speakers near the Volga in 1236.
Bulgars settled where the Kama meets the Volga in the 8th century.
Chuvash, the one surviving language of the Bulgar branch of Turkic.
Kazan Tatar grew from Bulgar and Kipchak speech under the Golden Horde.
Astrakhan Tatars and Nogais.
Nogai herders between the Volga and the Emba, pushed out by Kalmyks and Kazakhs.
The Lesser Nogai, between the Don and the Kuban.
Ibn Fadlan met Bashkirs on his way to the Bulgars in 922.
The taiga of the Ob and the Irtysh, thinly peopled. The early area is inferred from the languages.
Khanty on the Ob and Mansi on its western tributaries. Both are now small minorities.
Mansi lived west of the Urals too, on the upper Kama and the Pechora, until Russian settlement.
The tundra from the Ob to the Yenisei. Reindeer hunters and later herders, very thinly spread.
Taymyr, the land of the Nganasan and Enets. The Arctic islands inside this circle had no people.
The tundra west of the Urals. The Primary Chronicle names the Samoyad in 1096, and whether Samoyedic speakers were here much earlier is uncertain.
Novaya Zemlya and Franz Josef Land had no settled people. Nenets and Russian hunters visited Novaya Zemlya.
Selkup, on the middle Ob and the Taz.
Kamas and Mator, Samoyedic languages of the Sayan mountains that died out by the 20th century.
River names show that Yeniseian languages were once spoken across southern Siberia. Kott, Arin and Assan died out in the 18th and 19th centuries.
Ket, on the middle Yenisei, the last language of the family.
The taiga east of the Yenisei, very thinly peopled. The languages are unknown, and Yeniseian or other Old Siberian languages are assumed.
The Angara country west of Lake Baikal. The languages are unknown.
Tungusic reindeer hunters reached the Yenisei at an uncertain date, here put about 1200. Very thinly peopled.
A Turkic language close to Yakut, formed on Taymyr in the 18th century. Very thinly peopled.
The upper Yenisei, where runiform inscriptions of the Kyrgyz stand. Khakas and Tuvan are spoken here now.
The Altai and its foothills. Chinese histories place the first Turks here before 552, and Altai and Teleut are spoken here now.
The Kurykan, placed west of Lake Baikal by the Tang histories and taken to be Turkic.
Western Buryats of the Angara.
Tatars of the Tobol, the Irtysh and the Baraba steppe.
The Arsacid homeland, with old royal seats at Nisa and Hecatompylos.
Parthian noble houses such as the Karen and the Mihran kept their lands under the Sasanians.
Persis, whose kings struck their own coins under Parthian overlords.
Ardashir of Persis overthrew the Parthians in 224, and Persians ruled the empire from then on.
Most Persians became Muslim between the 8th and the 10th century and kept their language. They are about half the people of Iran today.
A kingdom in the hills above Susa, heir to ancient Elam. Its coins and inscriptions are in Aramaic, and what its people spoke is not known.
A kingdom in north-western Media. The name became Azerbaijan.
The Gorgan plain. Hyrcania broke away from Parthia for a time in the 1st century.
Gondophares made himself independent in Sistan and Arachosia about 19 and took the Kabul valley and Gandhara.
After the Kushans took the east, the line held Sistan until the Sasanians.
Dabuyids, Bavandids and other houses held the Caspian mountains. The Dabuyids, who fell in 761, were the last Zoroastrian rulers in Iran.
Governors of Khurasan for the Abbasid caliphs, at Nishapur, and in practice hereditary rulers.
Yaqub the coppersmith rose in Sistan and took Khurasan, Fars and Kabul.
Beaten by the Samanids in 900, the house kept Sistan.
Rulers of Transoxiana and Khurasan from Bukhara. New Persian literature began at their court.
Daylamite soldiers from the Caspian mountains who took western Iran and, in 945, Baghdad.
Turkic slave soldiers of the Samanids founded a state at Ghazni. Mahmud raided India from here.
After losing Khurasan to the Seljuks in 1040 they kept Ghazni and the Punjab.
Chiefs of the mountains of Ghor who burned Ghazni and conquered as far as Bengal. The speech of Ghor is said to have differed from Persian.
The White Sheep Turkmen confederation, which took Iran from its rivals the Qara Qoyunlu in 1467 and ruled from Tabriz.
Nader Shah, of the Turkic Afshar, drove out the Afghans, made himself shah and sacked Delhi in 1739.
After his murder his heirs kept Khurasan.
Karim Khan, of a Lak people of the Zagros, ruled most of Iran from Shiraz.
Arab writers name Kurds across the Zagros. In early texts the word often means mountain herders in general.
The Kurds of Iran. The Ardalan princes ruled from Sanandaj until 1867.
Herders of the southern Zagros. Their atabegs ruled Greater and Lesser Lur from the 12th to the 16th century.
Mountain people above the Caspian, foot soldiers for the Sasanians and later for themselves. Procopius names them.
The people of the Caspian shore, under local houses until the Safavids took Gilan and Mazandaran in the 1590s.
The geographers place the Baloch in Kerman. They moved east in the following centuries.
Makran and Sistan. Most Baloch live across the border in Pakistan.
Afghans appear in al-Biruni and the Ghaznavid histories around the Sulaiman range. Afghan is the older outside name.
The Durrani and Ghilzai confederations spread over the south and gave Afghanistan its rulers from 1747.
Mirwais Hotak threw off Safavid rule at Kandahar in 1709. His son took Isfahan in 1722 and ended the Safavid state.
Persian-speaking Shia of the central mountains, partly of Mongol descent. Babur names them, and they lost much land in the conquest of the 1890s.
A Turkic-speaking confederation of Fars, formed under the Safavids.
The Mushasha ruled from Hoveyzeh from 1436, and the Banu Kab followed. The province was long called Arabistan.
Turkic speakers of Azerbaijan, the home of the Safavid movement. They are the largest minority in Iran.
Arab armies took Merv in 651 and settled garrisons there. Qutayba took Bukhara and Samarkand by 712, and the Abbasid revolution began here in 747.
City states of the Zarafshan under their own lords, with Samarkand the first among them. The Chinese call the country Kang.
The Arabs crushed the last Sogdian rising in 722. Under the Samanids the Sogdians became Persian-speaking Muslims.
The Tashkent oasis, Shi in Chinese. It struck its own coins from the 3rd century.
The Dayuan of the Han histories, a land of walled towns and prized horses, later under its own kings until the Arab conquest.
A kingdom on the lower Amu Darya with its own era and script. Al-Biruni lists its Afrighid kings at Kath.
Under the Mamunids and then Turkic governors, the Khwarazmshahs. The Mongols destroyed Urgench in 1221.
Trading towns such as Suyab, Navekat and Talas, along the Chu and the Talas under Turkic rule.
Nomads from the borders of China who conquered Bactria about 130 BCE and divided it among five chiefs. Their language is disputed.
Kujula Kadphises, chief of one Yuezhi division, united the five and took Kabul and Gandhara.
Under Kanishka the empire ran from the Amu Darya to Mathura on the Ganges plain. Bactrian was its language of state.
After the Sasanians took Bactria, Kushan kings kept Gandhara and the Punjab for about a century.
Tokharistan, a land of small principalities under Sasanian, Hun, Turkic and then Arab overlords. Their legal documents survive.
Kings of Kabul of Turkic descent, who held off the Arabs for two centuries. A Hindu line followed them.
Kings of Zabulistan, south of the Hindu Kush, who worshipped the god Zun. The Saffarids overthrew them in 870.
Turkic speakers used the name Tajik for the Persian-speaking townsmen and farmers of the oases.
Tajiks of Bukhara, Samarkand, the upper Amu Darya and northern Afghanistan. Tajikistan was made a Soviet republic in 1929.
The people of Shughnan, Wakhan and the neighbouring valleys. Xuanzang names both, and most Pamiris are Ismaili today.
A mountain principality under its own mirs, known for rubies and lapis lazuli, until Afghanistan absorbed it.
The Parthian Stations calls the country Sakastan. The name survives as Sistan.
A nomad power on the middle Syr Darya with towns under its protection, known from Chinese report. Its language is assumed from names.
Herders of the Ili valley and Issyk-Kul, allies of Han China by marriage. Their language is not known.
Nomads east of the Caspian. The Parni, from whom the Parthian kings came, were one of their divisions.
Strabo places the Upper Aorsi along the Caspian and says they carried Indian and Babylonian goods by camel. The Alans replaced them.
The Sai of the Han histories, living among the Wusun. Burial mounds around Issyk-Kul are of Saka type.
Huns who took Bactria and then Gandhara, perhaps the Chionites whom Ammianus saw fighting beside the Persians in 359. Their kings took the Kushan title.
Procopius calls them White Huns. From Bactria they ruled Sogd, killed the Persian king Peroz in 484, and were broken by Persians and Turks about 560.
Hephthalite princes lasted in Badghis and Tokharistan until the Arab conquest.
Kings of Kapisa and Kabul, known from coins with a bull-headed crown. Xuanzang visited their court.
Byzantine writers say the Sabirs drove the Oghur peoples west about 463 and later appear north of the Caucasus. Their earlier home is a guess, and the name may live on in Siberia.
The western wing of the Turk khaganate, under Istemi and his heirs, with a court near Suyab. A Roman envoy reached it in 569, and Tang China broke it in 659.
After the Turgesh, the Karluks held Semirechye. The Kara-Khanid house came from among them.
The Oghuz under their yabgu, with a winter town at Yangikent near the mouth of the Syr Darya. The Seljuks were one of their clans.
A confederation on the Irtysh, described by the Persian geographers. The Kipchaks were its western division.
The Kipchaks took the steppe from the Irtysh to the Volga in the 11th century. Their western wing is the Cumans of European sources.
A khaganate on the lower Volga with its capital at Itil, whose rulers took up Judaism. Sviatoslav of Kiev destroyed it about 969.
The first Muslim Turkic dynasty, from Balasagun and Kashgar. They took Bukhara from the Samanids in 999.
The western khanate, at Samarkand, under Seljuk and then Kara-Khitai overlords.
Khitans who fled west when their Liao state fell in north China. From Balasagun they ruled Muslim Turks and beat the Seljuk sultan Sanjar in 1141.
The Jiankun of the Han histories. The Tashtyk culture of the Minusinsk basin is usually linked with them, and their language then is uncertain.
A Turkic-speaking kingdom on the upper Yenisei. In 840 it destroyed the Uyghur khaganate in Mongolia, and in 1207 it submitted to the Mongols.
Hulegu, a grandson of Chinggis Khan, destroyed the Assassins and Baghdad and ruled Iran from Tabriz and Maragha. Ghazan became Muslim in 1295.
The share of Chagatai, second son of Chinggis Khan, from the Amu Darya to the Altai. It split about 1347 into Transoxiana and Moghulistan.
The eastern, nomad half of the Chagatai realm. Its Turkic-speaking Muslim rulers still called themselves Mongols.
The eastern wing of the Golden Horde, under the line of Orda, eldest son of Jochi. Sources call it the White Horde or the Blue Horde and do not agree which.
Abulkhayr Khan united the nomads of the eastern steppe, who were called Uzbeks. The Kazakhs broke away from him, and his grandson led the rest to Transoxiana.
Herders between the Volga and the Emba under the heirs of Edigu, with their centre at Saraychik. The Kalmyks drove them west.
A successor of the Golden Horde on the middle Volga. Ivan IV took Kazan in 1552 and Astrakhan in 1556.
A Tatar khanate on the Tobol and the Irtysh that took tribute from the Khanty and Mansi. Yermak's Cossacks took its capital in 1582, and Khan Kuchum fought on until 1598.
Janibek and Kerei led their people away from the Uzbek khan about 1465. The khans later sat at Turkistan on the Syr Darya.
The Junior Zhuz, in the west. It took Russian protection in 1731.
The Middle Zhuz, in the centre and north. Russia abolished its khan in 1822.
The Senior Zhuz, in Semirechye, under Dzungar and then Kokand pressure before Russian rule.
Under Russian and Soviet rule. The famine of 1930 to 1933, which followed forced settlement, killed more than a third of the Kazakhs.
Shaybani Khan's Uzbeks took Transoxiana from the Timurids by 1507. The khanate passed from the Shaybanids to the Janids in 1599.
The Manghit emirs. A Russian protectorate from 1868, ended by the Red Army in 1920.
An Uzbek khanate in Khwarezm. A Russian protectorate from 1873.
A khanate of the Fergana valley that reached to Tashkent and the Syr Darya. Russia annexed it in 1876.
The name of the nomad conquerors of 1500 was given in 1924 to the settled Turkic speakers of the oases as a whole.
First recorded on the lower Syr Darya about 1600.
They moved to the Amu Darya delta in the 18th century. Karakalpakstan is an autonomous republic of Uzbekistan.
Mountain herders of the Tian Shan, under Moghul, Dzungar and Kokand overlords and Russian rule from the 1860s.
Oghuz who stayed east of the Caspian and became Muslim were called Turkmen.
Teke, Yomut, Ersari and other divisions, with no state of their own. Russia took Geok Tepe in 1881 and Merv in 1884.
The Oirat khanate, centred on the Ili beyond the present border. Its raids drove the Kazakhs west in 1723, and the Qing destroyed it in the 1750s.
Torghut Oirats who crossed the steppe to the lower Volga about 1630. Their khanate served the tsars until most of the people left for Dzungaria in 1771.
Those west of the Volga stayed. They were deported in 1943 and returned from 1957.
Hillforts between the Oka and the Volga, and the cemeteries that follow them, are taken as the work of the ancestors of the Mordvins.
The Pyanobor culture and its successors on the Kama. They are taken as ancestors of the Udmurts and Komi.
Jordanes names the Mordens and the Primary Chronicle the Mordva. Erzya and Moksha are their own names.
Under Moscow from the 16th century and scattered widely along the Volga since.
The Cheremis of the Russian chronicles, subject to the Bulgars, to Kazan and then to Moscow.
Between the Kama and the Vyatka. Votyak is the older Russian name.
The Perm of the chronicles, who paid tribute in furs to Novgorod.
Stephen of Perm baptised the Komi and wrote their language in the 1370s and 1380s. Zyryan is the older Russian name.
The friars call this country Great Hungary. Julian found people there in 1236 whose speech he understood, shortly before the Mongols came.
A trading state where the Kama meets the Volga. Its ruler took Islam and received the caliph's embassy in 922, and the Mongols conquered it in 1236.
Under the Golden Horde the Bulgar towns went on, and their people merged into the Kazan Tatars and the Chuvash.
First named in Russian records in the early 16th century.
Herders of the southern Urals, met by Ibn Fadlan in 922.
They accepted Moscow's rule in the 1550s and rose against it several times down to 1775.
The Muslim Turkic speakers of the former Khanate of Kazan.
Horse-breeding people of the forest edge on the Tobol and the Irtysh. Some scholars see the ancestors of the Hungarians among them, and that is not agreed.
Hunters and fishers of the middle Ob, known for cast bronze figures. They are often taken as early Samoyedic speakers.
The Yugra of the Primary Chronicle, beyond the mountains, who traded furs with Novgorod. Ostyak is the older Russian name.
Fishers and hunters of the Ob under their own princes, who paid fur tribute to Russia from the 1590s.
On both slopes of the Urals. The Pelym princes fought Moscow in the 15th century, and Vogul is the older Russian name.
East of the Urals only, on the Sosva and the Konda.
Reindeer people of the tundra from the White Sea to the Yenisei, very thinly spread. The chronicle calls them Samoyad.
The Russians met them on the middle Ob as the Piebald Horde, which resisted until 1598. Many later moved north to the Taz.
Hunters and fishers of the middle Yenisei, now a very small people.
Tobol, Irtysh and Baraba Tatars after the fall of the Khanate of Sibir.
Teleuts and other Turkic speakers of the Altai, under the Dzungars until 1756 and then Russia.
Turkic speakers of the Minusinsk basin who stayed when the Dzungars moved most of the Yenisei Kyrgyz away in 1703. The name Khakas was adopted in the 1920s.
Turkic-speaking herders of the upper Yenisei, under Mongol and then, from 1757 to 1911, Qing rule as Tannu Uriankhai.
A people's republic from 1921 and part of the Soviet Union from 1944.
The Arsacid kings ruled from Ctesiphon on the Tigris, in Mesopotamia, over a loose empire of vassal kingdoms from the Euphrates to Merv.
Founded by Ardashir of Persis in 224, with its capital at Ctesiphon. Arab armies broke it between 636 and 651.
Oghuz Turks under the house of Seljuk beat the Ghaznavids in 1040 and took Baghdad in 1055. The east held together until the death of Sanjar at Merv in 1157.
Turkic governors of Khwarezm for the Seljuks, the Khwarazmshahs made themselves independent.
For a generation they ruled from the Syr Darya to the Zagros. Chinggis Khan destroyed the state between 1219 and 1221.
Timur, a Turkic-speaking noble of the Barlas near Samarkand, conquered from Delhi to Ankara.
His heirs kept Transoxiana and Khurasan, with courts at Samarkand and Herat, until the Uzbeks took both.
Shah Ismail took Tabriz in 1501 with Turkmen followers and made Twelver Shia Islam the faith of the state. Isfahan was the capital from 1598.
A Turkmen house that reunited Iran from Tehran. It lost the Caucasus to Russia by 1828 and Herat to the Afghans.
Under the Pahlavi shahs from 1925 and an Islamic republic since the revolution of 1979.
Ahmad Shah Durrani was chosen king at Kandahar in 1747 and ruled from Khurasan to the Punjab. Kabul became the capital in the 1770s.
An emirate at Kabul. Its borders were drawn by Russia and Britain between 1873 and 1895, and Britain controlled its foreign affairs from 1879 to 1919.
A kingdom until 1973, then a republic and four decades of war. The Taliban have governed since 2021 and few states recognise their government.
Russia took the Khanate of Sibir by 1598 and reached the Yenisei by 1620. Siberia has been part of the Russian state, and of the Soviet Union from 1922 to 1991, ever since.
Russia took Tashkent in 1865 and made it the seat of a governor-general. Bukhara and Khiva stayed as protectorates.
An autonomous republic within Russia from 1920 and a union republic from 1936.
Made in 1924 when Moscow divided Turkestan, Bukhara and Khiva into republics named for nations.
Part of the Uzbek republic from 1924 and a union republic from 1929. Samarkand and Bukhara, with many Tajik speakers, stayed in Uzbekistan.
An autonomous republic from 1926 and a union republic from 1936.
Independent since 1991. The capital moved from Almaty to Astana in 1997.
Independent since 1991.
Independent since 1991.
Independent since 1991, with a civil war from 1992 to 1997.
Independent since 1991.
Aorsi and Alans between the Volga, the Urals and the Aral Sea.
Between the Don and the Volga.
The Hou Hanshu says that Yancai, north of the Aral Sea, took the name Alan. Ammianus has the Alans reaching far to the east.
Before they crossed the Volga about 370. Where the Huns came from, and whether they descend from the Xiongnu, is not settled.
Constantine Porphyrogenitus says the Pechenegs first lived between the Volga and the Ural river, until Oghuz and Khazars drove them west.
The lands of Batu and his heirs east of the Volga, with Khwarezm. The capital, Sarai, stood on the lower Volga.

One chain of dialects, among them Pitjantjatjara, Martu Wangka and Pintupi. Linguists think it spread across the desert within the last two thousand years, so the early extent is assumed. The land was thinly peopled.
The Nullarbor and its fringes, Mirning and Wangkatha country. Very thinly peopled, and placed loosely.
Arrernte and its relatives around the MacDonnell Ranges, recorded from the 1870s and still spoken by children.
Kaytetye and Alyawarr country to the north.
Warlpiri, Gurindji and their relatives from the Tanami Desert to the Victoria River. Warlpiri is one of the strongest Australian languages today.
A Pama-Nyungan group in north-east Arnhem Land, surrounded by unrelated languages. It is still the first language of its communities.
Yindjibarndi, Ngarluma, Banyjima and other Pama-Nyungan languages of the north-west, recorded from the 1860s.
Wajarri, Badimaya and the other Kartu languages of the Murchison and Gascoyne.
Nyangumarta and Karajarri country, behind the Eighty Mile Beach. Still spoken.
Yindjibarndi and Banyjima are still spoken in the inland Pilbara, beside English.
The dialects of the Noongar people, recorded from the 1820s at King George Sound and the Swan River.
Ngadju and Mirning country toward the Bight. Thinly peopled and placed loosely.
Noongar was still spoken in camps and on reserves in the early 20th century. It is being taught again today.
Kaurna, Narungga, Barngarla, Adnyamathanha and their neighbours around the South Australian gulfs. German missionaries wrote down Kaurna about 1840.
Wirangu and Kokatha country on the west coast of South Australia, thinly peopled.
Adnyamathanha stayed in daily use in the Flinders Ranges. Kaurna has been revived from the mission records.
The Kulin languages and their neighbours in what is now Victoria. Pama-Nyungan, though some linguists doubt how the south-eastern groups relate to each other.
Wiradjuri and its relatives on the inland rivers of New South Wales.
The Sydney language, Dharug, Dharawal and the Yuin languages of the coast. Dawes wrote down the Sydney language about 1790.
Gamilaraay, Bundjalung and the languages of New England and the north coast. Bundjalung and Gamilaraay are taught again today.
Ngarrindjeri and the other languages of the lower Murray.
Paakantyi, the language of the Darling River.
Inland languages were still spoken on stations and reserves for a generation or two after settlement.
Diyari, Arabana, Wangkangurru and their relatives in the Lake Eyre basin. Thinly peopled desert, tied together by long trade routes.
The Maric languages of inland Queensland, among them Bidjara. A convenience grouping of several Pama-Nyungan branches.
The Waka-Kabic and Durubalic languages of the south-east corner, around Moreton Bay.
Dyirbal and the rainforest languages behind Cairns and Townsville.
Kalkatungu and the Mayi languages of the Gulf country.
Still spoken on stations and settlements after the pastoral frontier had passed.
The Paman languages of Cape York, which give the Pama-Nyungan family the first half of its name. Dozens of languages in a small area.
Wik Mungkan, Kuku Yalanji and Guugu Yimithirr are still spoken, beside English and Cape York Creole.
The language of the western and central Torres Strait islands. Pama-Nyungan with a strong Papuan layer. Torres Strait Creole is now widely spoken beside it.
The language of Mer and the eastern Torres Strait islands, related to the Papuan languages of the Fly River mouth.
Gunwinyguan languages such as Bininj Kunwok, with Iwaidjan and the Maningrida languages on the coast. Not Pama-Nyungan. Several are still learned by children.
Several small families between Darwin and the Fitzmaurice River. Murrinh-patha at Wadeye is still the first language of its people.
A language with no known relatives, spoken on Bathurst and Melville Islands.
Bardi, Nyikina, Yawuru and their relatives on the Dampier Peninsula and the lower Fitzroy. Dampier landed here in 1688 and named no one.
Now spoken mainly by older people. Kriol and English are the everyday languages.
The Worrorran languages of the north Kimberley, the country of the Wanjina paintings.
Bunuba, Gooniyandi and the Jarrakan languages such as Gija and Miriwoong.
Now spoken mainly by older people. Kriol is the first language of most Kimberley Aboriginal communities.
Jingulu, Wambaya and the other Mirndi languages of the Barkly Tableland. Thinly peopled.
Garrwa and the Tangkic languages of the southern Gulf and the Wellesley Islands, with Pama-Nyungan Yanyuwa among them.
Perhaps a dozen languages, known only from word lists made between 1777 and the 1840s. Their relation to each other and to mainland languages cannot be shown.
After the removals of the 1830s the languages were spoken by a few survivors and in the Bass Strait islands. Fanny Cochrane Smith recorded songs about 1900. Palawa kani is a modern revival.
The convict colony at Sydney Cove, founded in January 1788.
The Cumberland Plain, the Hunter and, after 1815, the country beyond the Blue Mountains.
Squatters with sheep took the inland south-east within a generation. Gold in 1851 brought hundreds of thousands more.
Hobart, settled in 1803.
All of Tasmania after the war of the 1820s.
The Port Phillip District from 1835, the colony of Victoria from 1851.
Adelaide and the settled districts of South Australia. German was also spoken in the Barossa.
The farming and pastoral country of South Australia.
The Swan River Colony, small and slow to grow until the gold rushes.
The south-west and the goldfields after the rushes of the 1890s.
Geraldton, the Murchison and the Gascoyne.
The pastoral and, from the 1960s, mining country of the Pilbara. Aboriginal languages are still spoken here too.
The Moreton Bay penal settlement, later Brisbane.
Southern Queensland and the Darling Downs.
New England and the northern rivers of New South Wales.
The Queensland coast and its hinterland, opened by cattle, gold and sugar.
Cairns, Cooktown and the far north coast.
The sheep and cattle country of western Queensland, thinly peopled.
Mount Isa and the Gulf country, thinly peopled.
The Lake Eyre basin, with very few people of any language.
Darwin, founded as Palmerston in 1869.
Alice Springs, a small telegraph station until the railway came in 1929.
An English-based creole, which is why it is coloured as English. It grew from cattle station pidgin and became a first language at the Roper River mission after 1908.
The Barkly and the southern Gulf, where Kriol and English replaced most local languages.
Kriol spread into the Kimberley in the mid 20th century.
Dani, Mek, Ok and their relatives. Trans-New Guinea is a reconstructed family, and its spread along the highlands may go with early farming, though this is not settled.
The Paniai Lakes languages of the Mee and Moni.
Enga, Huli, Melpa, Kuman and the Kainantu and Goroka languages. Kuk swamp in the Wahgi valley shows drained gardens thousands of years old.
The Madang, Finisterre and Huon Peninsula languages.
Asmat, Kamoro and Awyu languages of the southern swamps and rivers. Thinly peopled away from the rivers.
The Ok languages around the head of the Fly and the Digul.
Binanderean, Koiarian, Goilalan and other families of the south-east peninsula, placed in Trans-New Guinea with varying confidence.
The Dagan and Mailuan languages toward the tail of the island.
The Sepik, Lower Sepik, Ramu and Torricelli families, among them Iatmul and Abelam. Several unrelated families share this basin.
The Ramu valley.
The Lakes Plain, Tor, Kwerba and Sentani languages of the Mamberamo basin and the north coast. Many small families and thinly peopled swamp, so the placing is loose.
The Sko and Border languages on both sides of today's frontier.
The West Papuan and East Bird's Head families, among them Maybrat and the Arfak languages. They are related to languages of Halmahera and not to the highlands.
The Bomberai Peninsula, where some languages are placed in Trans-New Guinea and Austronesian is spoken on parts of the coast.
Marind, the Trans-Fly families and Kiwai. Classification is disputed, and some of these are placed in Trans-New Guinea.
The Gulf of Papua, with the Eleman languages and several isolates.
Biak, Waropen, Wandamen and other Austronesian languages of the bay. They are the nearest relatives of Oceanic and not Oceanic proper, and are coloured with it for want of a closer key.
Austronesian languages of the Aru Islands. They belong with the languages of Maluku and are coloured with western Indonesia for want of a closer key.
The Kei Islands.
The Tanimbar Islands.
New Britain. Oceanic languages have been spoken in the Bismarck Archipelago since the Lapita expansion about three thousand years ago, which pottery sites date.
New Ireland and its offshore islands.
Manus and the Admiralty Islands.
Mussau, where some of the earliest Lapita sites were found.
Buka and the north of Bougainville.
The small atolls north of Bougainville, some of them Polynesian in speech.
The languages of central and southern Bougainville, such as Nasioi and Buin. They are older on the island than Oceanic.
Baining and its neighbours in the mountains of the Gazelle Peninsula.
Yélî Dnye of Rossel Island, a language with no known relatives.
Milne Bay, the D'Entrecasteaux and Trobriand Islands. Oceanic speakers settled here within the last three thousand years.
Woodlark Island.
The Louisiade Archipelago.
Motu, Mekeo and Roro on the coast around today's Port Moresby. Pottery shows coastal settlement here about two thousand years ago.
The Huon Gulf and the Markham valley, with Jabêm, Bukawa and Adzera.
Manam, Karkar and stretches of the Madang coast, beside Papuan neighbours.
Umboi and the Siassi Islands, traders across the Vitiaz Strait.
Malay was a trade language on the Onin and Bird's Head coasts under Tidore's influence. Few spoke it at home, so this is a thin claim.
Indonesian and Papuan Malay in Sorong, Manokwari and Fakfak. Since 1963 many settlers have come from other islands.
Jayapura and the north-east coast.
Merauke and its settlement areas.
Timika and Nabire, which grew with mining.
An English-based creole, which is why it is coloured as English. It took shape among plantation workers and settled around Rabaul in German times.
The common language of the Bismarck Archipelago under Australian rule.
The Sepik and the Madang coast, carried home by returning labourers.
Lae and the Huon Gulf.
Bougainville.
The highlands took up Tok Pisin after the 1950s. Local languages remain the home languages.
Port Moresby. Before independence the common language of Papua was Hiri Motu, a simplified Motu.
The coastal clans of Sydney Harbour, among them Gadigal and Cammeraygal. Projected back from 1788. Archaeology shows people here for many thousands of years.
Named in the First Fleet journals. Smallpox in 1789 killed perhaps half the people around the harbour. Their descendants live in Sydney today.
People of the three rivers, the Lachlan, Macquarie and Murrumbidgee. Projected back from where they were first recorded.
Recorded after Bathurst was founded in 1815. Martial law was declared against them in 1824.
Also Gamilaraay or Gomeroi. People of the Namoi and Gwydir plains, projected back from where they were first recorded.
Recorded by surveyors and squatters in the 1830s. The Myall Creek massacre of 1838 took place on the edge of this country.
An alliance of five peoples around Port Phillip, among them Wurundjeri and Boonwurrung. Projected back from 1835.
Recorded from the founding of Melbourne in 1835 and in the Port Phillip Protectorate papers.
Builders of the eel traps and channels at Budj Bim, parts of which are dated to more than six thousand years ago. The name is projected back and the works are not.
Recorded in the 1840s, when they fought settlers in the Eumeralla war.
People of the Murray and Goulburn river forests, projected back from where they were first recorded.
Recorded by squatters in the 1840s. Their walk-off from Cummeragunja mission in 1939 was an early mass protest.
People of the northern rivers, from the Clarence to the Logan. Projected back from where they were first recorded.
Recorded when cedar cutters and squatters arrived about 1840.
People of the lower Murray, the lakes and the Coorong. Projected back from where they were first recorded.
Recorded from about 1840 and at the Point McLeay mission, founded in 1859.
People of the Adelaide plains, projected back from 1836.
Recorded when Adelaide was founded in 1836. Missionaries wrote down the language, which has been revived from their work.
Also Paakantyi, the people of the Barka, the Darling River. Projected back from where they were first recorded.
Met by Mitchell's expedition in 1835. Native title was recognised in 2015.
The people of the south-west, in about fourteen dialect groups. Projected back from where they were first recorded.
Recorded at King George Sound from 1826 and the Swan River from 1829. Yagan led resistance near Perth in the 1830s.
A regional self-name for the peoples of the Murchison and Gascoyne, among them Wajarri and Badimaya. Projected back, and the shared name may be recent.
Recorded as pastoralists moved north of Geraldton from about 1850.
People of the Fortescue River tablelands in the Pilbara, near the rock engravings of Murujuga. Projected back from where they were first recorded.
Recorded after Roebourne was founded in 1866.
With Yankunytjatjara, the Aṉangu of the country around Uluru and the Musgrave Ranges. The start date is a guess, since Western Desert speech is thought to have spread in the last two thousand years.
Met by Giles and Gosse in 1873. Freehold title to the Aṉangu Pitjantjatjara lands was granted in 1981.
People of the Great and Little Sandy Deserts. Placed loosely, with a start date that is a guess.
Met along the Canning Stock Route from 1906. Some families lived wholly in the desert until the 1960s.
People of the MacDonnell Ranges and Mparntwe, now Alice Springs. Projected back from where they were first recorded.
Recorded from the building of the telegraph in 1872 and at Hermannsburg mission from 1877.
People of the Tanami Desert, projected back from where they were first recorded.
Recorded as miners and cattlemen entered the Tanami. Many were killed in the Coniston massacre of 1928.
Also Dieri. People of Cooper Creek east of Lake Eyre, projected back from where they were first recorded.
Recorded at the Lutheran mission at Killalpaninna from 1866.
The people of north-east Arnhem Land. Projected back from later records.
Yolŋu song, art and loanwords record generations of trade with Makassan trepang fleets.
Recorded at missions from 1923. The Yirrkala bark petitions of 1963 began the modern land rights cases.
People of the stone country and floodplains of western Arnhem Land, whose rock art spans thousands of years. The name is projected back.
Recorded at Oenpelli, now Gunbalanya, in the early 20th century.
People of Bathurst and Melville Islands. Dutch ships met islanders here in 1705 without naming them.
They resisted the British post of Fort Dundas from 1824 until it was abandoned. A mission came in 1911.
The saltwater people of Darwin harbour, projected back from 1869.
Recorded when the town of Palmerston, now Darwin, was surveyed in 1869.
People of the upper Victoria River, projected back from where they were first recorded.
Recorded after Wave Hill station was set up in 1883. Their walk-off in 1966 led to the first land hand-back in 1975.
People of Roebuck Bay, projected back from where they were first recorded.
Recorded when Broome grew up as a pearling port in the 1880s, with divers from across Asia.
People of the limestone ranges of the central Kimberley, projected back from where they were first recorded.
Recorded as cattle stations arrived in the 1880s. Jandamarra led their resistance from 1894 to 1897.
Rainforest people of the Daintree and Bloomfield rivers, projected back from where they were first recorded.
Recorded during the Palmer River gold rush from 1873.
People of the Endeavour River, projected back from 1770.
Cook's crew spent seven weeks here in 1770 and wrote down words of the language, among them kangaroo. A Lutheran mission followed in 1886.
The Wik peoples of western Cape York. Jansz met people on this coast in 1606, the first recorded European landing in Australia, and Wik tradition recalls Dutch visits.
Recorded at Aurukun mission from 1904. The Wik judgment of 1996 held that native title can coexist with pastoral leases.
Also Kalkatungu. People of the ranges around today's Mount Isa, projected back from where they were first recorded.
Recorded from the 1860s. They fought settlers and police for years, until a defeat at Battle Mountain in 1884.
With Turrbal, the people of the Brisbane River. Projected back from 1825.
Recorded from the founding of the Moreton Bay penal settlement.
People of the Carnarvon Ranges and the upper Warrego, a country rich in stencil art. Projected back from where they were first recorded.
Recorded after Mitchell's expedition of 1846 opened the country to squatters.
Tasmanian Aboriginal people, in about nine nations. Archaeology shows people here for some forty thousand years, cut off from the mainland for the last twelve thousand.
Met by French and British ships from 1772. Settlement from 1803 led to the Black War of the 1820s and the removal of survivors to Flinders Island.
The claim that they died out in 1876 was false. The community, also called Pakana, descends mainly from families of the Bass Strait islands.
A community descended from Palawa women and sealers on Cape Barren and Flinders Islands. They spoke English with Palawa words and kept the people alive, and they are Palawa.
Western Torres Strait Islanders of Mabuiag, Badu and Moa. Torres sailed through in 1606 and named no one. Archaeology shows island villages and gardens for well over two thousand years.
Recorded from the arrival of the London Missionary Society in 1871, which Islanders mark as the Coming of the Light.
The people of Mer, Erub and Ugar in the eastern strait, gardeners under the law of Malo. The name is projected back.
Described by passing ships about 1800 and by missionaries from 1871. Eddie Koiki Mabo's case over Mer land brought the recognition of native title in 1992.
The largest language group in Papua New Guinea. Enga oral history reaches back to the coming of sweet potato about 1700 and the growth of the tee exchange. Earlier placement is assumed.
First met by prospectors and patrols between 1934 and 1938.
People of the Tari basin, with long genealogies. Projected back from 1935.
First met by the Hides and O'Malley patrol in 1935.
People of the Mount Hagen area, where Kuk swamp shows gardening for thousands of years. The name is projected back and the farming is not.
First met by the Leahy brothers and Taylor in 1933. Known for the moka exchange.
Also Simbu, speakers of Kuman, in some of the most densely gardened valleys of the island. Projected back from 1933.
First met by the 1933 patrol through the Wahgi valley.
Farmers of the Baliem valley. Projected back from where they were first recorded.
The Baliem valley and its tens of thousands of people became known to outsiders in 1938, though Dutch expeditions had met western Dani earlier.
Also Ekari or Kapauku. People of the Paniai Lakes, projected back from 1936.
The lakes were sighted from the air in 1936 and a Dutch post followed.
People of the middle Sepik, known for their great ceremonial houses. Projected back from where they were first recorded.
Recorded by German river expeditions about 1912.
Yam growers of the hills north of the Sepik. Projected back from where they were first recorded.
Recorded by patrols and ethnographers from about the 1930s.
Seafarers of Biak and Numfor in Cenderawasih Bay. Projected back from later records.
Biak sailors raided and traded as far as Maluku and carried tribute to Tidore, as their own traditions and European reports agree.
Recorded by missionaries from 1855.
Hatam, Meyah, Sougb and Moile of the Arfak Mountains. Projected back from where they were first recorded.
Recorded by naturalists who climbed from Doreh Bay in the 1870s.
Woodcarvers of the southern tidal swamps. Cook's men landed on this coast in 1770 and were driven off, without learning who lived there.
Recorded by Dutch expeditions in the early 20th century. A permanent post came only about 1938.
Also Marind-anim. People of the southern coast and savanna, whose language some place in Trans-New Guinea. Projected back from 1902.
The Dutch founded Merauke in 1902 to stop Marind raids across the border.
People of the Fly River mouth, traders with Torres Strait. Their language is placed in Trans-New Guinea by some. Projected back from the 1870s.
Recorded by missionaries and river explorers from the 1870s.
Potters and sailors of the coast around today's Port Moresby. Their hiri voyages carried pots west to the Gulf for sago. How old the hiri is remains debated.
Recorded from the arrival of the London Missionary Society in 1874.
People of the plain behind Yule Island, with hereditary chiefs. Projected back from where they were first recorded.
Recorded by the Sacred Heart mission from the 1880s.
People of the plains north of the Owen Stanley Range. Projected back from where they were first recorded.
Recorded during the gold rushes of the 1890s. The name was applied by outsiders and later taken up.

An archaeological label and not a people's name. The island communities that descend from the Lapita voyagers of about three thousand years ago, known from pottery, obsidian trade and their Oceanic languages.
People of the Gazelle Peninsula. Tradition and language suggest their forebears crossed from New Ireland, perhaps after the great Rabaul eruption of the 7th century. The start date is a guess.
Recorded by traders and Methodist missionaries from 1875. Known for tabu shell money.
The people of Kiriwina and its neighbours, partners in the Kula exchange ring. The outside name comes from a French officer of 1793. Projected back from the 1890s.
Recorded by missionaries from 1894 and by Malinowski from 1915 to 1918.
Peoples of the Admiralty Islands, among them the sea-going Titan. Obsidian from here was traded widely in Lapita times. The peoples are projected back.
Recorded by visiting ships from the 1870s and under German rule.
People of central Bougainville, speaking a Papuan language. Projected back from where they were first recorded.
Recorded by Marist missionaries about 1902. The Panguna mine on their land was at the centre of the Bougainville conflict of 1988 to 1998.

Fleets from Makassar in Sulawesi camped each wet season on the Arnhem Land coast to gather and cure trepang. The trade was running by about 1700 and some argue for an earlier start. Australian law ended it in 1907.

The Sultan of Tidore in Maluku claimed tribute from the Raja Ampat islands and the Bird's Head and Onin coasts. The reach was loose. The Dutch built their own claim on it and took direct control about 1898.
A British penal colony from 1788. It claimed the eastern half of the continent and held little of it.
The colony before Victoria and Queensland were separated.
Self-governing from 1856.
Settled from Sydney in 1803 and a separate colony from 1825. Renamed Tasmania in 1856.
The Swan River Colony of 1829. For decades it held only the south-west corner of the third of the continent it claimed.
Founded in 1836 without convicts. It also governed the Northern Territory from 1863 to 1911.
Separated from New South Wales in 1851, the year gold was found.
Separated from New South Wales in 1859. Its frontier was among the most violent.
The six colonies federated in 1901. Aboriginal people were counted in the Commonwealth after the 1967 referendum, and native title was recognised in 1992.
The Netherlands claimed the western half of the island in 1828. It kept no lasting post until 1898 and reached the highlands only in the 1930s.
The north-east of the island and the Bismarck Archipelago, annexed by Germany in 1884 and taken by Australian troops in 1914.
A British protectorate over the south-east from 1884, annexed in 1888 and passed to Australia in 1906.
British New Guinea under Australian rule.
Former German New Guinea, under Australian military rule from 1914 and a League of Nations mandate from 1921. Japan held much of it from 1942 to 1945.
The two Australian territories joined under one administration.
Independent since 1975, with English, Tok Pisin and Hiri Motu as national languages. Bougainville voted for independence in 2019 and its status is still being negotiated.

Indonesia has governed western New Guinea since 1963, confirmed by the disputed Act of Free Choice of 1969. It is now several provinces. An independence movement contests this and the atlas does not settle it.
The Prakrit of Gandhara, written in Kharoshthi script on stone, birch bark and coins. It went out of written use by about 400.
The Kashmir valley. Kashmiri is written from about the 13th century and its earlier presence is inferred.
Shina, Khowar and Kohistani in Gilgit, Chitral and the upper Indus gorges.
Ladakh and Baltistan before Tibetan spread there. The land was thinly peopled and the placement is loose.
Dardic and Punjabi-like speech in Swat and the Peshawar valley, before Pashto speakers took the plain.
A language with no known relatives. A wider early range in the Gilgit region is assumed from place names. The land was thinly peopled.
Hunza, Nagar and Yasin.
Tibetan speech spread west to Ladakh with the Tibetan empire in the 7th and 8th centuries. Thinly peopled high desert.
Balti, the westernmost Tibetan language.
The Sulaiman range. Pashto or its ancestor is assumed here. Nothing is written in it before the 16th century.
Al-Biruni places the Afghans in the mountains west of the Indus about 1030.
Yusufzai and other Pashtun clans settled the Peshawar valley and Swat in the 15th and 16th centuries.
Quetta, Pishin and Zhob.
The languages of early Balochistan are unknown. Brahui, a Dravidian language, is shown as the candidate, though some scholars think it arrived from central India only about 1000. Thinly peopled.
The Kalat highlands.
Baloch moved east from Kerman and Sistan into Makran from about 1000. Thinly peopled desert and coast.
Baloch clans reached the Kachhi plain and the Indus in the 15th century.
The Prakrit of the lower Indus, from which Sindhi grew.
Arab writers of the 10th century note a language of Sindh distinct from that of Multan.
Urdu speakers from north India settled in Karachi at Partition in 1947. Urdu is also the state language of Pakistan.
Shauraseni and related Prakrits of the Ganges and Yamuna plain, and the Apabhramsha that followed them. Inscriptions at Mathura and elsewhere are in Prakrit until about 300.
Punjab and Haryana.
Rajasthan. The Thar desert was thinly peopled.
Malwa, around Ujjain and Vidisha.
Braj, Awadhi, Khari Boli and their neighbours. Hindi and Urdu are two written standards of the speech of Delhi.
Malvi and Bundeli.
Haryana and Delhi.
Bagheli, spreading into hills where Gondi and Munda languages were spoken.
Marwari, Mewari and Dhundhari. Old Rajasthani and Old Gujarati were one written language until about 1400.
Written from about the 12th century.
Saraiki, around Multan.
Pothohari and Hindko.
The western Himalaya. Indo-Aryan speakers called Khasas are assumed here beside Tibeto-Burman speakers. Thinly peopled mountains.
