Dogri, Kangri, Garhwali, Kumaoni and their neighbours.
The Khas language of the Karnali basin in western Nepal, in inscriptions from the 13th century.
Khas speakers spread east through the middle hills.
Eastern Nepal, after the Gorkha conquest.
Darjeeling and Sikkim, settled by Nepali speakers in the 19th century.
Tibeto-Burman languages of the Nepal hills: the ancestors of Magar, Gurung, Tamang, Newar and the Kiranti languages. Early placement rests on where they are spoken later.
Still the languages of much of the central and eastern hills, beside Nepali.
Lepcha and Limbu in Sikkim.
The western Prakrit and Apabhramsha from which Gujarati grew.
Written from about the 12th century.
Kutch, where Kutchi, a language closer to Sindhi, is spoken beside Gujarati. The salt flats of the Rann are thinly peopled.
The Bhil hills. What the Bhils spoke before they took up Indo-Aryan is unknown.
Bhili, an Indo-Aryan language close to Gujarati and Rajasthani.
The Prakrit of the western Deccan, used in Satavahana inscriptions and in verse.
Vidarbha, with Gondi in the hills around.
The Konkan coast.
Marathi appears in inscriptions from about 1000.
Vidarbha.
Konkani on the coast and in Goa.
Indo-Aryan speech in the plain of the upper Mahanadi, where kings issued Sanskrit charters from the 6th century.
Chhattisgarhi spread out from the plain into Gond country.
Central Dravidian languages are assumed to have held the hills between the Narmada and the Godavari. Nothing was written in them.
Gondwana, the country of the Gond kingdoms.
Bastar, Gadchiroli and Mandla, where Gondi is still spoken.
Kui and Kuvi, the languages of the Kondh hills.
Kurukh, spoken by the Oraon of Chota Nagpur. Their tradition says they came from the west.
Munda languages are assumed to have reached well beyond Chota Nagpur. The evidence is their later range and loanwords in Indo-Aryan.
The Chota Nagpur plateau.
Mundari, Ho and Santali.
Santals settled the Rajmahal hills from the 1790s.
The hills behind the Kalinga coast.
Sora, Gutob and Bonda.
Korku in the Satpura hills, the westernmost Munda language.
Magadhi, the Prakrit of Bihar, and the Apabhramsha that followed it.
Western and northern Bengal.
Eastern Bengal, where land grants to Brahmins begin in the Gupta period.
The Kalinga coast.
The languages of Bihar, eastern Uttar Pradesh and the Nepal plain.
Sadri and Magahi spread onto the plateau among Munda speakers.
The oldest Bengali verse is of about 1000.
Eastern Bengal.
Northern Bengal.
Chittagong.
Sylhet and the Barak valley.
Odia appears in inscriptions from about 1050.
Sambalpur and the upper Mahanadi.
Ganjam and the southern hills.
Xuanzang found the speech of Kamarupa a little different from that of mid India.
The lower Brahmaputra valley.
Upper Assam. The Ahom court had gone over to Assamese by about 1700.
The speech of the eastern delta before Indo-Aryan is not known. Tibeto-Burman is shown, and Austroasiatic is also argued.
Bodo-Garo languages of the Brahmaputra valley. Many river names in Assam are from them.
Garo in the hills and Bodo and Rabha on the north bank.
Dimasa and Karbi.
Kokborok in Tripura.
The Chittagong hills. Thinly peopled. The Marma and Chakma of today arrived from Arakan after 1500.
The language of the Ahoms, who crossed from upper Burma in 1228. It gave way to Assamese and survives only in ritual.
An Austroasiatic language far from its relatives. Its long presence on the plateau is inferred.
The Naga hills and the Manipur valley. Meitei is written from about the 11th century.
The Lushai hills. Mizo speakers came from the east about 1700 and replaced related languages.
The eastern Himalaya south of Tibet. Thinly peopled, and unrecorded before the 19th century.
Assumed from the later range. Inscriptions here are in Prakrit until the 4th century.
The first Kannada inscription is of about 450.
A 9th century Kannada work says the language was spoken from the Kaveri to the Godavari.
Northern Karnataka, after Marathi took the country to the north.
A Dravidian language of the coast around Mangalore. It is its own branch and is filed with Kannada here for convenience.
Telugu names appear in Prakrit inscriptions of the Krishna valley from the 2nd century.
The first Telugu inscriptions are of about 575.
Telangana, with Gondi to the north.
Telangana.
The coast north of the Godavari.
Rayalaseema and Nellore.
Tamil has been written in the far south since before 1 CE, in cave inscriptions and then in the Sangam poems.
The northern Tamil country around Kanchipuram.
The west coast, part of the Tamil country in the Sangam poems.
Southern Kerala.
The western dialect of Tamil became a separate language between about 900 and 1300.
Southern Kerala.
An Indo-Aryan language brought by sea from north India some centuries before 1 CE. Cave inscriptions in early Sinhala Prakrit are found across the island.
The south and the hill country.
The old dry zone heartland, thinly peopled after its reservoirs were abandoned in the 13th century.
Tamil speakers were present in the north beside Sinhala speakers. How many, and from when, is disputed.
The north has been mainly Tamil-speaking since the time of the Jaffna kingdom.
The east coast.
Tamil workers brought from south India to the tea estates of the hills.
The language of the island's forest hunters. Its original form is lost and what survives is heavily mixed with Sinhala.
The eastern forests.
The Maldives were settled by speakers of an early form of Sinhala. The date is uncertain and may be a few centuries after 1 CE.
Copper plate grants in Dhivehi survive from the 12th century.
Saka kings of the line of Azes in Gandhara and Punjab, known from coins. The Indo-Parthians replaced them about 20.
The Northern Satraps at Mathura, who outlasted them until the Kushans came.
A warrior republic between the Sutlej and the Yamuna, known from its coins. Samudragupta's pillar inscription lists it among those who submitted.
The Rai kings and then the Brahmin line of Chach, with their capital at Aror. The dates come from a late source.
Conquered for the Umayyad caliphate by Muhammad ibn al-Qasim in 712.
The Habbari emirs of Mansura. A separate emirate held Multan.
Kings of Gandhara and Punjab, with their seat at Hund on the Indus after losing Kabul. The Ghaznavids destroyed the kingdom.
The Soomras, a local line in lower Sindh. Little contemporary record survives.
The Sammas of Thatta.
The Kalhoras and, from 1783, the Baloch Talpur emirs ruled Sindh until the British conquest of 1843.
Arab accounts of the conquest of Sindh describe the Zutt as herders of the lower Indus.
By Mughal times the Jats were the main farming people of Punjab, Haryana and the upper Yamuna.
Baloch tradition and the evidence of the language bring them east from Kerman into Makran after 1000.
Baloch clans on the Kachhi plain and along the Indus. Balochistan today is divided between Pakistan and Iran.
Herders of the Kalat highlands who speak a Dravidian language. When they came there is disputed.
A confederacy of Brahui and Baloch clans under the Ahmadzai khans. It acceded to Pakistan in 1948.
The Khalsa was founded in 1699. From the 1750s Sikh war bands, the misls, held most of Punjab between them.
Most Sikhs moved to the Indian side of Punjab at Partition in 1947.
Ranjit Singh took Lahore in 1799 and went on to take Multan, Kashmir and Peshawar. The Company annexed the kingdom in 1849.
The people of the five rivers. Partition in 1947 divided Punjab between Pakistan and India, and millions crossed the new line.
Saka rulers of Gujarat and Malwa. The Periplus names one at Barygaza, Ptolemy names another at Ujjain, and their dated coins run for three centuries. Their inscriptions are in Prakrit and Sanskrit.
A republic of eastern Rajasthan known from small copper coins. The region of Malwa to the south later took their name.
Kings of Mandsaur in Malwa. Yashodharman's pillar inscription claims the defeat of the Huna king Mihirakula about 528.
Kings of Valabhi in Saurashtra, first as Gupta governors. Xuanzang visited their city.
They rose in Rajasthan and Malwa and stopped Arab armies advancing from Sindh.
From Kannauj they ruled most of the north. Arab writers call the king of Juzr the strongest enemy of Islam in India.
A remnant around Kannauj, sacked by Mahmud of Ghazni in 1018.
The Chahamanas of Shakambhari and Ajmer. They took Delhi from the Tomaras about 1150 and lost it to the Ghurids in 1192.
Kings of Malwa at Dhar. Bhoja, who died about 1055, is the best known.
Kings of Bundelkhand and builders of the Khajuraho temples.
Kings of Tripuri near Jabalpur, in the hill country between the Ganges plain and the Deccan.
The Chaulukyas of Anhilwara in Gujarat, followed by the Vaghelas. Delhi conquered the kingdom about 1304.
The Guhila kings of Chittor. Their early history rests partly on later bardic tradition.
The Sisodia kings, the leading Rajput house. Their capital moved to Udaipur after 1568.
The Rathor kingdom of the western desert. Jodhpur was founded in 1459. The early dates are from bardic chronicles.
The Kachhwaha kingdom. Its kings served the Mughals as generals from 1562 and built Jaipur in 1727.
The people of Gujarat, long known as traders across the Indian Ocean.
Kings with names ending in mitra, known only from coins found around Ahichchhatra.
Local kings of the city of Kaushambi on the Yamuna, known from coins and a few inscriptions.
Kings of Padmavati and Mathura after the Kushans withdrew. The Puranas name them, coins confirm them and Samudragupta claims to have uprooted them.
The Guptas rose in Magadha and the middle Ganges. Samudragupta's pillar inscription at Allahabad lists the kings he conquered.
At its height the empire ran from Gujarat to Bengal. Faxian travelled through it and found it peaceful and lightly governed.
After the Huna invasions the Guptas held only the east.
Kings of Kannauj after the Guptas.
The Pushyabhuti kings of Thanesar.
Harsha ruled the north from Kannauj for forty years. Xuanzang knew him. The empire did not outlast him.
Kings of Kannauj and Varanasi, defeated by the Ghurids in 1194.
Kharavela's inscription near Bhubaneswar records a conquering king of Kalinga. Its date is disputed between the 1st century BCE and the 1st CE. Pliny names the Calingae.
Kingdoms of the eastern delta. Samudragupta's inscription names Samatata as a frontier kingdom and Xuanzang visited it.
Shashanka of Gauda, the first king to unite Bengal and the enemy of Harsha.
The kingdom of the Brahmaputra valley under three successive dynasties. Xuanzang stayed with its king Bhaskaravarman. The court used Sanskrit and most subjects did not.
Buddhist kings of Bengal and Bihar. Dharmapala and Devapala fought the Pratiharas and Rashtrakutas for Kannauj.
The later Palas, patrons of the great monasteries of Nalanda and Vikramashila.
A dynasty of southern origin that replaced the Palas. Turkish cavalry took their western capital about 1204.
Kings who moved from the upper Mahanadi to the coast and built the great temples of Bhubaneswar.
The early Gangas of Kalinganagara on the border of the Telugu country.
Anantavarman Chodaganga took the whole Odisha coast. His line built the temples of Puri and Konark.
Kings of Odisha who for a time held the coast from the Ganges to the Kaveri.
Tai-speaking Ahoms crossed the Patkai hills from upper Burma in 1228 and founded a kingdom in upper Assam.
The kingdom took the whole valley and beat back the Mughals in 1671. Its court took up Assamese and Hinduism. Burma and then the Company ended it.
Founded by the Koch chief Bishwa Singha. Its western half survived as the princely state of Cooch Behar.
Mughal governors at Murshidabad who ruled in their own right. The Company defeated the nawab at Plassey in 1757 and took the revenue in 1765.
Bengal was divided in 1947 between India and East Pakistan, which became Bangladesh in 1971.
The people of Odisha, under Afghan, Mughal, Maratha and British rule in turn after 1568.
The people of the Brahmaputra valley.
A people of the Himalayan foothills known from silver and copper coins. Ptolemy's Kulindrine is probably their country.
Later chronicles say Kirata kings ruled the Nepal valley before the Licchavis. The name is used in Sanskrit for hill peoples in general.
Kings of the Kathmandu valley whose Sanskrit inscriptions begin in 464. Many place names in them are in an early form of Newar.
Buddhist kings of Gilgit, known from inscriptions and manuscripts and from Chinese accounts of Little Balur. Their language is not known.
The Karkota, Utpala and Lohara kings. Lalitaditya raided far into the plains about 740.
The Katyuri kings.
The Chand kings of Kumaon and the Panwar kings of Garhwal. Gorkha armies conquered both by 1804.
Known mainly from its own later royal chronicle. A kingdom founded by a branch of the old Tibetan royal house, under the Namgyal kings from 1460. The Dogras of Jammu conquered it by 1842.
The Khasa Malla kings of the Karnali basin, who also held western Tibet for a time. Their language became Nepali.
Newar kings of the Kathmandu valley, divided after 1482 among Kathmandu, Patan and Bhaktapur.
A small hill kingdom whose king Prithvi Narayan Shah conquered the Kathmandu valley in 1768 and 1769.
A kingdom of Bhutia rulers over Lepcha and later Nepali subjects. It joined India in 1975.
The people of the valley under Mughal, Afghan, Sikh and Dogra rule. Since 1947 sovereignty over Kashmir has been disputed between India and Pakistan.
Independent of Delhi from about 1342, with capitals at Pandua and Gaur. The sultans patronised Bengali as well as Persian.
The Shah Mir sultans and the Chaks. Most Kashmiris became Muslim in this period. Akbar annexed the valley in 1586.
The Sharqi sultans of the middle Ganges, rivals of Delhi until the Lodis absorbed them.
Sultans of Mandu.
Sultans of Ahmedabad, rich from the sea trade of Cambay. Akbar conquered the kingdom in 1573.
Nawabs of Faizabad and Lucknow, Mughal governors who became kings. The Company annexed Awadh in 1856.
Pashtun soldiers who made a state east of Delhi. A remnant survived as the state of Rampur.
The Nizams, Mughal viceroys of the Deccan who became its kings and then the largest princely state. Their subjects spoke Telugu, Marathi and Kannada.
Nawabs of Arcot, over whose succession the British and French fought. The Company took over in 1801.
Kings of the western Deccan with their seat at Paithan. The Periplus knows the elder Saraganus. The Puranas list them as Andhras, with reign lengths that do not agree.
Under Gautamiputra and his successors they held the Deccan from sea to sea. Ptolemy names Siriptolemaios at Baithana.
Successors of the Satavahanas in the Krishna valley, with their capital at Nagarjunakonda.
Kings of Vidarbha and the northern Deccan, allied to the Guptas by marriage. The later Ajanta caves were cut under them.
Kings of Banavasi. The earliest Kannada inscription dates from their time.
Kings of southern Karnataka at Talakad, usually under a stronger neighbour. The Cholas ended the kingdom.
Kings of the Krishna and Godavari deltas.
Pulakeshin II stopped Harsha at the Narmada about 620. Xuanzang describes his kingdom.
A branch of the Chalukyas in the Telugu deltas, where written Telugu took shape. The line merged with the Cholas.
Kings of Manyakheta who raided north to the Ganges and south to the Kaveri. Arab merchants called their king the Balhara and ranked him among the great kings of the world.
They restored Chalukya rule over the Deccan and fought the Cholas for a century and a half.
Kings of southern Karnataka at Dwarasamudra, builders of the temples of Belur and Halebidu.
Kings of Warangal who joined the Telugu uplands and the coast. Delhi's armies took Warangal in 1323.
Kings of the Marathi country, under whom Marathi became a written language. Delhi annexed the kingdom in 1317.
An empire of the whole south founded at Hampi on the Tungabhadra. Portuguese visitors describe the city at its height about 1520.
After defeat by the sultanates at Talikota in 1565 the kings ruled from Penukonda and Chandragiri.
The Wodeyar kings, at first under Vijayanagara.
Under Hyder Ali and Tipu Sultan Mysore fought four wars with the Company.
A princely state under the restored Wodeyars.
Shivaji was crowned at Raigad in 1674.
Under the Peshwas of Pune and the houses of Sindhia, Holkar, Bhonsle and Gaekwad the Marathas held or taxed most of India. The Afghans defeated them at Panipat in 1761.
The Company broke the confederacy in the wars of 1803 and 1817.
The Marathi-speaking people of Maharashtra.
The Kannada-speaking people, joined in one state in 1956.
The Telugu-speaking people of the coast and the uplands.
Founded by officers who rebelled against Delhi, with capitals at Gulbarga and Bidar. It fought Vijayanagara for the land between the Krishna and the Tungabhadra.
The Nizam Shahi sultans.
The Adil Shahi sultans. Dakhni, an early literary form of Urdu, was written at their court.
The Qutb Shahi sultans, who founded Hyderabad in 1591 and also patronised Telugu.
A governor of Delhi who made himself sultan. Ibn Battuta stayed at the court. Vijayanagara ended it.
Kings of the west coast and the pepper trade. Pliny and the Periplus know the king as Caelobothras or Cerobothra, and the port as Muziris.
The later Cheras of Mahodayapuram.
The early Cholas of the Kaveri delta, with their port at Kaveripattinam.
The line revived at Thanjavur under Vijayalaya.
The imperial Cholas under Rajaraja and Rajendra held the south and northern Sri Lanka, and raided the ports of Sumatra and Malaya in 1025.
The later Cholas, until the Pandyas absorbed the kingdom.
Kings of Madurai. Pliny names King Pandion and the inland city of Modura.
The first Pandya empire, rivals of the Pallavas.
The later Pandyas were the richest kingdom of the south until Delhi's armies sacked Madurai in 1311.
Chiefs of the far south-west, the Aioi of Ptolemy. Their country later became Venad.
Rulers of the Tamil country in a period with almost no records. They are known from later inscriptions of the kings who overthrew them.
The early Pallavas of Kanchipuram, whose charters are in Prakrit and Sanskrit.
The great Pallavas, builders of Mamallapuram. Xuanzang visited Kanchipuram about 640.
The kingdom of Venad, around Kollam.
Martanda Varma enlarged it into Travancore, which lasted as a princely state.
The Zamorins, lords of the pepper port where Ibn Battuta saw Chinese junks and where Vasco da Gama landed in 1498.
Telugu-speaking governors of Vijayanagara who became kings of the southern Tamil country.
The Tamil-speaking people of the south, whose name for their country is as old as the Sangam poems.
The people of Kerala.
The Sinhalese kingdom of the northern plain, built on great reservoirs. Pliny records its embassy to Rome and Faxian lived there for two years. A Chola army took the king in 1017.
The south of the island, often under its own princes and a refuge for kings driven from the north.
Vijayabahu drove out the Cholas in 1070. Parakramabahu I, who died in 1186, ruled the whole island.
Sinhalese kings withdrew to the wet south-west and moved their capital several times.
A Tamil kingdom of the north under the Arya Chakravarti kings. Ibn Battuta met its king in 1344. The Portuguese conquered it in 1619.
The kingdom of the south-west coast. The Portuguese arrived in 1505 and inherited the crown in 1597.
The hill kingdom that held out against the Portuguese and the Dutch. The British deposed its last king in 1815.
Forest hunters, the island's oldest population. The chronicle's stories of them are legend, and the placement is loose. The name is the Sinhala one. They call themselves Wanniyala-Aetto.
Knox described them in the eastern forests in 1681. A few communities remain.
The islands' Buddhist king became a Muslim sultan in 1153 by the traditional date. Ibn Battuta served as a judge there in 1343.
The majority people of Sri Lanka.
The Tamils of the north and east. A civil war over a separate Tamil state lasted from 1983 to 2009.
Placed by their language and by later record. No early source that names them can be located. They call themselves Koitur.
The largest of the hill peoples of central India.
Garha-Mandla, Deogarh, Kherla and Chanda. Akbar's general defeated queen Durgavati of Garha in 1564. The Marathas took the last of them.
Placed where they are found later. Their early language is unknown.
Sanskrit writers name the Bhillas as hill archers from about 600. Rajput kings of Mewar were installed with Bhil rites.
Peoples of the Chota Nagpur plateau. Their own traditions and their language are the evidence before the 18th century.
Placed by language and tradition on the eastern edge of the plateau.
The Company settled Santals in the Rajmahal hills from the 1790s. They rose against landlords and the Company in 1855.
A Dravidian-speaking people of Chota Nagpur, also called Oraon. Their tradition brings them from the Rohtas hills to the north-west.
Hill farmers of inland Odisha, called Khonds in older books. Recorded from the 1830s and placed earlier by language.
The Savaras of Sanskrit texts. Pliny's Suari and Ptolemy's Sabarai are probably the same name, though where those writers meant is not certain.
Placed by language. Naga is an outside name for some dozens of peoples with languages of their own.
The Ahom chronicles record wars and treaties with the Nagas from the 13th century.
Placed by language.
The Jaintia kingdom and the Khasi chiefdoms, annexed by the Company in the 1830s.
The Kachari kingdom of Dimapur and later Maibang and Khaspur, a neighbour and rival of the Ahoms.
The Meitei kingdom of the Imphal valley, also called Kangleipak. Its royal chronicle claims a far earlier beginning that cannot be checked.
The Manikya kings of the Tripuri, also written Twipra.
Mizo tradition brings them from the Chin hills about 1700. They were called Lushai in British records.
Peoples of the Arunachal hills, first described in the 19th century. China claims most of Arunachal Pradesh and the border is disputed.
Founded by Turkish officers of the Ghurids. It held the north from the Indus to Bengal.
Under the Khaljis and Muhammad bin Tughluq its armies reached Madurai. Ibn Battuta served as a judge in Delhi.
The provinces broke away, Timur sacked Delhi in 1398, and the Sayyid and Lodi sultans ruled only the upper Ganges.
Founded by Babur in 1526. The Afghan Sur kings drove out his son from 1540 to 1555. Akbar then took the north from Gujarat to Bengal.
By the death of Aurangzeb in 1707 the empire covered all but the far south.
The emperors kept the title and little else. The British deposed the last in 1857.
Goa, taken in 1510, with Daman, Diu and forts along the coast. India annexed Goa in 1961.
Portuguese rule on the coasts.
The Dutch East India Company took the Portuguese forts and held the coasts.
British from 1796, and the whole island from 1815.
The English company took the revenues of Bengal in 1765. It already held Madras and Bombay.
By conquest and by treaty with the princes the Company became master of India. The crown took over after the rising of 1857.
Provinces under the crown and more than five hundred princely states under treaty. It was partitioned into India and Pakistan in 1947.
The Dogra kings of Jammu bought Kashmir from the Company in 1846. Since 1947 the former state has been divided and its sovereignty disputed between India and Pakistan, with China holding part.
Made by the Gorkha conquests from 1768. A war with the Company in 1814 to 1816 fixed its borders. Never a colony.
Independent in 1947 and a republic from 1950, with states redrawn along language lines from 1956. Sovereignty over Kashmir is disputed with Pakistan, and parts of the northern border with China.
Created in 1947 from the Muslim-majority provinces of British India. Sovereignty over Kashmir is disputed with India.
East Pakistan, the eastern wing, which broke away in 1971.
Independent after the war of 1971.
Independent as Ceylon in 1948 and renamed in 1972.
A British protectorate from 1887, independent in 1965 and a republic from 1968.
The Yellow River plain, Chinese speaking throughout.
The Wei valley around Chang'an.
Eastern Gansu. Qiang and later Tibetan and Tangut speakers lived among the Chinese here.
Shandong and the tip of Liaodong.
Ningxia and the edge of the Ordos, irrigated by Han colonists. Steppe peoples held it for long periods.
The Hexi corridor, garrisoned from 121 BCE. Tibetan, Uyghur and Tangut rulers held it between about 780 and 1227.
Dunhuang and Jiuquan. The Dunhuang documents show a Chinese-speaking town under Tibetan and later local rule.
The Sichuan basin, settled from the north after 316 BCE.
The middle Yangzi, the old land of Chu.
The lower Yangzi.
Commandery towns along the Xiang and Gan rivers, with non-Chinese speakers in the hills around them.
Hunan and Jiangxi, filled by migrants from the north after 311 and again after 755.
Zhejiang, settled under the Wu kingdom and the Eastern Jin.
Fujian. Chinese settlement was thin before the Tang.
Panyu, now Guangzhou, a Chinese port city among Yue speakers.
Guangdong. Most of its Chinese population arrived under the Tang and Song.
Eastern Guangxi.
The coast of Hainan.
Guizhou, made a province in 1413 and settled by garrisons and then by farmers.
Yunnan, settled by Ming military colonies after 1382.
The hills north of Beijing.
Chinese farmers settled southern Inner Mongolia from the late 19th century.
South-eastern Inner Mongolia.
The Yellow River bend.
Northern Xinjiang, where settlement after 1949 made Chinese the majority language.
The Han commanderies of Liaodong and Liaoxi.
Liaodong and the coast road to it, Chinese farming country under the Yuan, the Ming and the early Qing.
The Qing opened Manchuria to Chinese settlement from 1860. Millions came from Shandong and Hebei.
The far north along the railway and the Amur.
The Yue of Zhejiang and Fujian. Their language is unrecorded. A link to Tai is the common view and an Austronesian link has also been proposed.
The Yue of Lingnan, inferred to be Tai speakers from the Tai languages still spoken in the west of the area and from Tai words in Cantonese.
Western Guangxi, where Zhuang is still the main rural language.
Bouyei, Kam and Sui in southern Guizhou.
The Hlai languages of the Li of Hainan.
Tai speakers spread into southern Yunnan about the 11th to 13th century.
The hill country south of the middle Yangzi. The Man peoples of the Chinese histories are taken to have spoken early Hmong-Mien, which is inference.
Western Hunan and eastern Guizhou, the Miao heartland.
Yao of the Nanling range.
Hmong moved west into western Guizhou and Yunnan in the 17th to 19th centuries.
The Yunnan plateau. The language of the Dian kingdom is unknown and Loloish speech is first described under Nanzhao.
The Liangshan hills, still Yi speaking.
Western Guizhou, held by Yi lords until the 17th century.
Austroasiatic speakers of south-western Yunnan before the Tai spread. Placement is inferred from where Wa, Bulang and Palaung are spoken now.
Wa and Bulang in the hills.
The hills where Hunan, Hubei and Chongqing meet. Tujia gave way to Chinese from the 18th century and few speakers remain.
The Qiang of the upper Yellow River and Kokonor, named throughout the Han histories.
The Qaidam basin and the Altun range, thinly peopled by Qiang herders.
The north-eastern plateau before Tibetan spread. Thinly peopled, and the languages are inferred.
The gorge country of western Sichuan, where Qiangic languages are still spoken in pockets.
Qiang and Gyalrong speakers on the upper Min river.
Naxi, Pumi, Lisu and Nu in the gorges of north-western Yunnan.
The language of the Western Xia, written in its own script from 1036. It died out under the Ming.
The Tsangpo valley, home of the Yarlung kings. Before the script of the 7th century this is reconstruction.
Central Tibet and Bhutan.
The Changtang, a high plain with very few people.
The headwaters of the Yangzi and the Yellow River, thinly peopled.
Western Tibet, where Tibetan replaced Zhangzhung after the conquest of the 640s.
Kham.
Amdo, taken from the Tuyuhun and the Qiang in the 7th century.
The Qaidam basin, thinly peopled.
Tibetan garrisons at Miran and around Lop Nor.
The language of the western plateau before Tibetan, known from a few texts and thought to be related to the West Himalayan languages.
Kucha, Karashahr and Turfan. The manuscripts date from about 400 to 800 and the language is assumed for the centuries before.
Loulan and Shanshan. The kingdom wrote in Gandhari Prakrit and its own language is uncertain, perhaps a third Tocharian language.
Khotan, Yarkand and Kashgar. Khotanese documents run from the 7th to the 10th century.
Sarikoli and Wakhi, eastern Iranian languages still spoken in the Pamirs.
Turfan, settled by Uyghurs from Mongolia after 840. Old Uyghur and modern Uyghur are different branches of Turkic.
Hami.
The Tarim basin. Kashgar was Turkic under the Karakhanids by about 960 and Khotan fell in 1006.
Lop Nor and Charkliq, desert with very few people.
The Wusun of the Ili valley. Nothing of their language survives. Iranian is the usual guess.
Western Mongolia and the Altai.
The Orkhon and Selenga. A few Xiongnu words survive in Chinese transcription and the language is unclassified.
Eastern Mongolia.
The Southern Xiongnu, settled along the Chinese frontier after 48.
The Greater Khingan and the upper Liao river. Wuhuan and Xianbei, then Khitan and Xi.
Western Mongolia under the Xianbei confederation.
The Xianbei took the Xiongnu lands in the 2nd century.
Eastern Mongolia.
The Tuoba and other Xianbei along the Chinese frontier.
Western Mongolia.
The Rouran language is unrecorded. Some scholars take it for early Mongolic.
Eastern Mongolia.
Dzungaria. Tiele and Gaoche, then Turks, Karluks, Basmyl and the Uyghurs of Beshbalik.
Western Mongolia. The Naimans of the 12th century may have spoken Turkic.
The Orkhon valley, centre of the Turk and Uyghur khaganates.
Eastern Mongolia.
Turks settled along the frontier by the Tang, then Shatuo and Öngüt.
The Kurykan around Lake Baikal, taken to be among the ancestors of the Yakuts.
The Argun and Hulun lake. The Shiwei here are taken to have spoken early Mongolic.
Mongolic speakers moved west onto the steppe after the Uyghur khaganate fell in 840.
Central Mongolia. Which of the Kereit and their neighbours spoke Mongolic and which Turkic is disputed.
Eastern Mongolia.
Central Mongolia.
Western Mongolia, Oirat speaking from the 15th century.
Inner Mongolia. Chinese has been the majority language of its farmed south since about 1900.
Dzungaria, Oirat land until the Qing destroyed the Dzungars in the 1750s.
The Khorchin and other eastern Mongols.
Oirat Mongols settled around Kokonor and the Qaidam in the 1630s.
Kazakh herders moved into the emptied Dzungar pastures after 1760.
The Sungari, Ussuri and lower Amur. Yilou and Mohe are taken to be Tungusic speakers, which is inference before the Jurchen script of 1119.
The coast range and the lower Amur, home of the Nanai and Udege.
The upper Amur and the northern Khingan, thinly peopled forest.
Central Manchuria under Balhae, the Jurchens and the Manchus. Manchu gave way to Chinese in the 19th century.
The Sanguozhi says Buyeo, Goguryeo, Okjeo and Ye spoke alike. Whether these languages were Koreanic is disputed.
Goguryeo on the Yalu.
Northern Korea. Chinese was also used in the Lelang commandery until 313.
The Okjeo of the north-east coast.
The Han languages of the south. Korean descends from the speech of Silla.
Jeju. Its early language is unknown and its speech today is a distinct form of Korean.
Silla joined the peninsula in 668 and its language spread north with Goryeo and Joseon.
The north-east, settled under King Sejong in the 1430s.
Mohe and Jurchen speakers held the north-east coast until Joseon pushed to the Tumen.
Place names recorded in the Samguk Sagi suggest a language related to Japanese was once spoken in parts of Korea. The evidence and its placement are disputed.
Kyushu, Shikoku and western Honshu. Japonic is taken to have arrived with Yayoi rice farming.
Western Japan.
Central Honshu and the Kanto plain.
Southern Tohoku.
Northern Tohoku, conquered by the court around 800.
Hokkaido, colonised from 1869.
Southern Sakhalin was Japanese from 1905 to 1945 and its settlers were then repatriated.
Northern Honshu. Place names of Ainu type are the evidence that the Emishi here spoke a related language.
Hokkaido. Ainu is recorded from the 17th century and assumed for the earlier cultures of the island.
Ainu moved into southern Sakhalin about the 13th century.
The Kuril Islands, very thinly peopled. Ainu are known here from about the 14th century and the earlier language is unknown.
The shell-mound peoples of Okinawa and Amami. Their language is unknown.
The southern Ryukyus had a separate prehistory with links to the south. The language is unknown.
Japonic speakers from Kyushu settled the islands about the 10th to 12th century. Japanese has largely replaced Ryukyuan since 1945.
Miyako and Yaeyama.
The forest east of Lake Baikal, thinly peopled. Northern Tungusic is thought to have spread from about here.
The upper Lena and Vitim. The early languages of this forest are unknown and Tungusic is assumed.
The Okhotsk coast, thinly peopled. Placement before the 17th century is inferred.
Evenki reindeer hunters spread across the Lena basin in the first and second millennium. Very thinly peopled.
Even herders in the mountains of the north-east, moving into Yukaghir land.
Yukaghir languages are thought to have reached from the Lena to the Anadyr before Tungusic and Yakut spread. Very thinly peopled, and it includes arctic islands with no settled people.
The Yana, Indigirka and Kolyma.
Yukaghir shrank to the Kolyma after the epidemics of the 17th and 18th centuries.
Chukotka, thinly peopled. Recorded from the 1640s and assumed earlier.
Kamchatka and the coast north of it. Koryak in the north and Itelmen in the south.
Koryak is still spoken in the north of Kamchatka.
Sea-mammal hunters of the Bering Strait coast, known from the Old Bering Sea culture onward.
The mouth of the Amur and northern Sakhalin.
All of Sakhalin before the Ainu came north. The Okhotsk culture is often linked to Nivkh, which is inference.
Turkic cattle and horse herders reached the middle Lena from the Baikal region about the 13th century.
Yakut spread north to the Arctic coast in the Russian period. Very thinly peopled.
Mongolic speakers on both sides of Lake Baikal.
The eastern Taimyr, tundra with almost no people. Samoyedic speech here before the 17th century is assumed.
Transbaikalia, settled by Cossacks and peasants after the forts of the 1650s.
Yakutsk and the Lena post road.
Kamchatka, where settlers and Itelmen merged.
The left bank of the Amur, Russian from 1858.
The Ussuri and the coast, Russian from 1860.
Northern Sakhalin.
Southern Sakhalin after 1945.
The Kuril Islands. Japan disputes Russian sovereignty over the four southern islands.
Russian became the majority language of the Lena basin in the 20th century. Very thinly peopled.
The north-east, settled around mines and ports under Soviet rule.
Chukotka.
Kamchatka and the Okhotsk coast.
The Okhotsk coast and the Stanovoy range.
The eastern Taimyr, almost without people.
The Yellow River plain, the core of the Han empire and of Mandarin speech today.
The lower Yangzi, the old lands of Wu and Yue. It became the richest part of China after the migrations of the 4th and 12th centuries.
Settled from the north after Qin took Shu in 316 BCE, and largely resettled from Hubei and Hunan after the wars of the 17th century.
Hunan and Jiangxi, where northern migrants and local peoples merged.
Fujian. Its speech keeps features older than those of other Chinese varieties.
The Pearl River delta. Cantonese took shape under the Tang and Song from northern speech and a Yue base.
The Western Han and the Xin interregnum of Wang Mang from 9 to 23. Capital at Chang'an.
The Eastern Han, with its capital at Luoyang.
The northern kingdom, founded by Cao Pi with its capital at Luoyang.
Founded by Liu Bei at Chengdu and conquered by Wei in 263.
The kingdom of the Sun family at Jianye, now Nanjing. Its campaigns against the Shan Yue opened the south-east to Chinese settlement.
The Western Jin, which reunited China in 280 and lost the north after 311.
The Eastern Jin at Jiankang, now Nanjing, a court of northern exiles ruling the south.
Founded by the Southern Xiongnu leader Liu Yuan. Its armies sacked Luoyang in 311.
Founded by Shi Le of the Jie, a people of the Xiongnu confederation. One line of their language survives and it is unclassified.
Founded by the Murong Xianbei of the Liao valley, who moved their capital south to Ye.
Founded by the Fu family of the Di. Under Fu Jian it held all north China until its defeat at the Fei river in 383.
Founded by the Yao family of the Qiang at Chang'an.
A state in the Hexi corridor under the Juqu family of the Lushuihu, a people of Xiongnu background. Its fall to Northern Wei in 439 ended the Sixteen Kingdoms.
The Tuoba Xianbei state with its capital at Pingcheng, now Datong.
It held all north China from 439. The court moved to Luoyang in 494 and took up Chinese speech and dress.
The eastern half of Northern Wei, ruled from Ye.
The western half of Northern Wei, ruled from Chang'an. It took Sichuan in 553 and the east in 577.
The first of the Southern Dynasties at Jiankang.
The second of the Southern Dynasties.
The longest reign of the south was that of Emperor Wu of Liang, from 502 to 549.
The last southern court, conquered by Sui in 589.
Sui reunited north and south in 589 and dug the Grand Canal.
Capital at Chang'an. Tang armies held the Tarim oases and the Mongolian steppe for parts of the 7th and 8th centuries.
After the An Lushan rising of 755 the Tang lost the west and much of its hold on the provinces.
Later Liang, Tang, Jin, Han and Zhou at Kaifeng and Luoyang. Three of the five were founded by Shatuo Turks.
The largest southern kingdom, on the lower Yangzi.
The Qian family's kingdom at Hangzhou.
A kingdom at Guangzhou that held Guangdong and Guangxi.
Two successive kingdoms at Chengdu.
The Northern Song, with its capital at Kaifeng.
The Southern Song at Hangzhou, after the Jurchens took the north.
Khubilai's dynasty, ruling China from Dadu, now Beijing. It took the Southern Song in 1279.
Capital at Nanjing and from 1421 at Beijing.
The Manchu dynasty took Beijing in 1644, Mongolia by 1691 and a protectorate over Tibet in 1720.
With the conquest of the Dzungars and the Tarim in the 1750s the empire reached its full extent.
Proclaimed in 1912 and governed from Beijing, then Nanjing, with much of the country under regional armies. Its government moved to Taipei in 1949.
The People's Republic of China, founded in 1949.
Han abolished the Min Yue kingdom in 110 BCE and the Shiji says its people were moved north. The hill population stayed outside Chinese rule.
The people of the former Nanyue kingdom, conquered by Han in 111 BCE and governed from commandery towns.
The Yue of Guangxi. The name also covers the Red River plain to the south.
The hill Yue of southern Anhui, Zhejiang and Jiangxi, fought and conscripted by the Wu kingdom.
Chiefdoms of Lingnan known for their bronze drums. Lady Xian of the Li brought them over to the Sui in the 6th century.
A kingdom on Lake Dian, known from its bronzes and from the gold seal Han gave its king in 109 BCE. Its language is unknown.
The Cuan family ruled eastern Yunnan for four centuries. The Tang called their peoples the Black and White Man.
A kingdom on Lake Erhai that defeated Tang armies in the 750s and raided Chengdu and Hanoi. Its rulers spoke a Loloish language and many of its people an early form of Bai.
The Buddhist kingdom of the Duan family, conquered by Khubilai in 1253.
The hill peoples of western Hunan, who rose against Han from 47. That they were ancestors of the Miao and Yao is inference.
Miao is a Chinese name. Hmong, Hmu and Qo Xiong are among the names the people use.
After the risings of the 18th and 19th centuries many moved west into Yunnan and on into Southeast Asia.
Hill farmers of the Nanling range between Hunan, Guangdong and Guangxi.
The Tai speakers of Guangxi, the largest minority people of China. Nong Zhigao led a rising against Song in 1052.
The Wuman and Luoluo of the Chinese histories, in the Liangshan hills, eastern Yunnan and western Guizhou. Nuosu is the name used in Liangshan.
The people of the Dali plain. Where the Bai language belongs within Sino-Tibetan is disputed.
Governed by their own hereditary chiefs until the 1720s. Most now speak Chinese.
The Tai Lue principality of Sipsongpanna, by tradition founded about 1180.
The people of Hainan. Han set up two commanderies on the island in 110 BCE and gave them up in 46 BCE.
The present-day Qiang of the upper Min river. They carry the ancient name, and the line of descent from the Qiang of the Han histories is not simple.
Herders of the upper Yellow River and Kokonor. Their wars with the Eastern Han ran through the 2nd century.
A kingdom of western Tibet, conquered by Songtsen Gampo in the 640s. Its early history is later tradition.
The kings of the Yarlung valley, known from the Old Tibetan Chronicle, which was written down later.
From Songtsen Gampo's unification the Tibetans held the whole plateau.
A kingdom around Kokonor founded by a branch of the Murong Xianbei over a Qiang population. Tibet destroyed it in 663.
The Dangxiang of the Sichuan and Qinghai border, who moved north to the Ordos under Tibetan pressure.
Tangut is the Mongol name. The people called themselves Mi.
The Tangut empire, with its capital at what is now Yinchuan. Chinggis Khan destroyed it in 1227.
A kingdom of western Tibet founded by descendants of the imperial line. Ladakh conquered it in 1630.
At its height it held the Tarim oases and the Hexi corridor and took Chang'an for a few days in 763.
The government of the Dalai Lamas at Lhasa, under Qing protection from 1720. Its standing between 1912 and 1951 is disputed.
United by Zhabdrung Ngawang Namgyal, who came from Tibet in 1616. A monarchy since 1907.
A Buddhist kingdom on the southern Silk Road, Saka speaking. The Karakhanids took it in 1006.
The oasis at the western end of the basin. Its language is thought to have been Saka.
The largest oasis of the northern rim, called Qiuci in Chinese. Its language is the one now called Tocharian B.
Home of Tocharian A, known as Agni in its own texts.
A kingdom around Lop Nor that kept its records in Gandhari Prakrit. Its own language is uncertain.
A kingdom at Turfan ruled by Chinese families over a mixed Chinese, Tocharian and Sogdian population. Tang annexed it in 640.
Uyghurs from Mongolia founded a kingdom at Turfan and Beshbalik. Its ruler submitted to Chinggis Khan in 1209.
A Uyghur kingdom in the Hexi corridor, conquered by the Tanguts. The Yugur of Gansu are taken to descend from it.
Founded by a Chagatai prince in 1514 and ruled in its last decades through the Khoja religious leaders. The Dzungars took it in 1680.
The Turkic Muslim people of the oases. They were named by their towns until the name Uyghur was taken up again in the 1920s.
The first steppe empire of Mongolia. It split into northern and southern halves in 48.
The Southern Xiongnu, who settled inside the Han frontier.
The Northern Xiongnu withdrew west after their defeat in 91 and then leave the Chinese record.
Herders of the Greater Khingan, once subject to the Xiongnu.
Under Tanshihuai the Xianbei took the whole of the old Xiongnu steppe.
After 235 they divided into the Murong, Tuoba, Yuwen and Duan, who founded states in north China.
The khaganate that held Mongolia against the Northern Wei. Its Turk subjects overthrew it in 552.
Turkic-speaking cart-dwellers. A Gaoche kingdom north of Turfan lasted from 487 to 541.
The Tiele of northern Mongolia, from whom the Uyghurs came.
The first Turk khaganate. This is its eastern half, which Tang conquered in 630.
The second khaganate, whose rulers set up the Orkhon inscriptions.
Ruled from Ordu-Baliq on the Orkhon. Its court adopted Manichaeism in 762.
From the upper Yenisei they sacked Ordu-Baliq in 840. Their hold on Mongolia was loose and brief.
A people of eastern Mongolia, called Zubu in Liao records. Temüjin destroyed them in 1202 and their name passed to others.
A Christian people of the Tuul and Orkhon. Whether they spoke Mongolic or Turkic is disputed.
A people of the Altai and western Mongolia with a Uyghur-style chancery. Their language is disputed.
The Mongols of the Onon and Kherlen before Temüjin was raised as Chinggis Khan in 1206.
Founded by Chinggis Khan. By 1260 it reached from Korea to the Black Sea and was dividing into four khanates.
The Chinggisid khans in Mongolia after the Ming took China. Dayan Khan reunited the eastern Mongols about 1500.
The western Mongols. Under Esen they captured the Ming emperor in 1449.
The last steppe empire. The Qing conquest of 1755 to 1758 killed or scattered most of the Dzungars.
The Mongols north of the Gobi, who submitted to the Qing in 1691 and are the majority in Mongolia today.
Chahar, Tümed, Ordos, Khorchin and other Mongols south of the Gobi, organised in banners by the Qing from 1636.
Declared independence from the Qing in 1911. A people's republic from 1924 and a multi-party state since 1990.
Herders settled along the Han frontier. Cao Cao broke them at White Wolf Mountain in 207.
Forest people east of Buyeo, whom the Chinese identified with the ancient Sushen. Their language is assumed to be Tungusic.
Called Wuji in the Weishu. The Sumo Mohe helped found Balhae and the Heishui Mohe of the Amur became the Jurchens.
Herders of the Xar Moron river. Their language, written in two scripts of their own, is a relative of Mongolic.
Peoples of the Argun and the northern Khingan. The Mengwu Shiwei of the Tang histories carry the first record of the name Mongol.
A kingdom of Mohe and Goguryeo people, called Bohai in Chinese. Korean and Chinese historians each claim it, and the language of its rulers is disputed.
The Khitan empire, which held Manchuria, Mongolia and the Beijing region.
Tungusic farmers and hunters of the Sungari. Under the Ming they were known as the Jianzhou, Haixi and Wild Jurchens.
The Jurchen empire, which destroyed Liao in 1125 and took north China from Song in 1127.
Hong Taiji gave the Jurchens the name Manchu in 1635. Ten million people are counted as Manchu today and almost none speak the language.
A Turkic people around Lake Baikal, named in the Orkhon inscriptions and known for their horses.
Sea-mammal hunters known from the Old Bering Sea and Punuk cultures, taken to be ancestors of the Yupik.
Villages on the coast of Chukotka.
Placement before the Russian records is inferred from the spread of the language.
Reindeer hunters spread very thinly across the forest. The Russians called them Tungus.
Reindeer herders of the Okhotsk coast and the Kolyma, formerly called Lamut.
The early extent is inferred from place names and from where the language was found in the 17th century.
Hunters of the Kolyma and Indigirka. Epidemics and absorption left a few hundred speakers.
Assumed from later records.
Reindeer herders and sea hunters who call themselves Luoravetlan. They fought off Russian forces through the 18th century.
Assumed from later records.
Northern Kamchatka and the coast of the Sea of Okhotsk.
Assumed from later records.
Fishers of the Amur mouth and northern Sakhalin, called Jilimi in Yuan records and Gilyak by the Russians.
Turkic horse and cattle herders on the middle Lena. Their own tradition and the language point to an origin near Lake Baikal.
The Russians founded Yakutsk in 1632. The Sakha then spread north and west.
The Secret History lists the Buriyad among the forest peoples who submitted in 1207.
A kingdom on the Sungari plain. Goguryeo and Baekje both claimed descent from it.
A kingdom in the hills of the middle Yalu.
It took Lelang in 313, moved its capital to Pyongyang in 427 and fell to Tang and Silla in 668.
A Han commandery at Pyongyang, founded in 108 BCE and governed by Chinese officials for four centuries.
Peoples of the east coast, subject to Goguryeo.
The largest of the three Han, a league of more than fifty communities in the south-west. Baekje grew from one of them.
Twelve communities east of the Nakdong. Silla grew from one of them, Saro.
Twelve communities on the lower Nakdong, known for their iron. They became Gaya.
A kingdom on the Han river. The traditional founding date of 18 BCE is not supported by other evidence.
Driven south by Goguryeo in 475. Tang and Silla destroyed it in 660.
A kingdom at Gyeongju. The traditional founding date of 57 BCE is not supported by other evidence.
Unified Silla held the peninsula south of the Taedong river.
A league of small states on the Nakdong. The Nihon Shoki's claim of a Yamato base here is disputed.
The island kingdom of Jeju, tributary to Baekje, Silla and Goryeo in turn.
One people under Goryeo and Joseon, divided between two states since 1948.
Founded by Wang Geon at Kaesong. It gave Korea its name and was a Mongol vassal from 1259 to 1356.
The Yi dynasty at Seoul, which fixed the border on the Yalu and Tumen. Styled the Korean Empire from 1897 and annexed by Japan in 1910.
The Democratic People's Republic of Korea. Each Korean state claims the whole peninsula.
The Republic of Korea. Each Korean state claims the whole peninsula.
The Chinese name for the people of the Japanese islands, living in many small communities. Where Queen Himiko's Yamatai lay, in Kyushu or in central Honshu, is disputed.
The kingship of the Nara basin, whose great tombs spread from Kyushu to the Kanto plain.
The people of southern Kyushu, who rose against the court for the last time in 720.
The people of the state ruled from Nara, Kyoto, Kamakura and Edo in turn.
Farmers and traders of the island chain. Local lords built stone castles called gusuku from the 12th century.
United from Shuri in 1429 and a trading partner of Ming China. Satsuma invaded in 1609 and Japan annexed the kingdom in 1879.
The court state with its capital at Nara and from 794 at Heian, now Kyoto.
Warrior government at Kamakura beside the court at Kyoto. It turned back Mongol fleets in 1274 and 1281.
The Ashikaga shoguns at Kyoto. From 1467 power lay with warring regional lords, until Nobunaga and Hideyoshi reunited the country after 1568.
Government from Edo, now Tokyo, over some 260 domains.
The Meiji state took in Hokkaido and Ryukyu, and southern Sakhalin in 1905.
Japan annexed Korea in 1910 and set up Manchukuo in Manchuria in 1932. The empire ended with defeat in 1945.
Under the constitution of 1947.
The hunters and fishers of Hokkaido who kept the Jomon way of life after rice farming spread through Honshu. Known from archaeology only.
The court's name for the people of northern Honshu beyond its rule. Their leader Aterui surrendered in 802.
Sea hunters of Sakhalin, the north coast of Hokkaido and the Kurils. Often linked to the Nivkh, which is inference.
Ainu culture took shape in Hokkaido about the 13th century. Japan annexed the island in 1869 and recognised the Ainu as an indigenous people in 2008.
Ainu of southern Sakhalin and the Kurils. The Yuanshi records wars with the Guwei of Sakhalin from 1264.
Sami languages across the far north of Fennoscandia. Thinly peopled land. Norwegian, Swedish, Finnish and Russian are now the majority languages in most of it.
Sami of the Kola peninsula, with Russian the majority language since the 19th century.
The Przeworsk and Wielbark cultures, usually linked with the Lugii, Vandals and Goths. The language is inferred from those names.
Slavic speech spread here in the 5th and 6th centuries. The evidence is archaeology and later languages.
The lower Oder and Pomerania.
The plain between the Danube and the Tisza before the Sarmatian Iazyges settled it in the 1st century.
The Moesi and their neighbours south of the Danube.
Gaulish among the Helvetii. Raetic, further east, was a separate and little-known language.
The Alamanni settled the upper Rhine from the 3rd century. Their speech became Swiss German and Alsatian.
Moselle Franconian, the speech of Luxembourg.
Provincial Latin on the upper Danube, which Bavarian German replaced in the 6th century.
The Kyiv culture, which most scholars link with early Slavic speech. The language is inferred.
Russian of the upper Volga and Beloozero.
After the Huns broke the Gothic kingdom in the 370s the Pontic steppe held Huns, Alans and others. What most people there spoke is not known.
River names show Baltic speech on the upper Dnieper and Oka before Slavic. The Galindians of the Protva were named as late as the 12th century.
Slavic speakers settled Wallachia, Moldavia and Transylvania from about 500. How much Romance speech lasted beside them is disputed, and this seed does not settle it.
Gaelic replaced Pictish and Norse in the far north and gave way to English in the 19th century.
English in the far north of Scotland.
English of the east Midlands and Lincolnshire, with much Norse in it.
English in Cumbria, replacing Cumbric and Norse.
Scots in the eastern Lowlands and up the coast.
English became the majority language of the west of Ireland in the later 19th century. Irish is still spoken in the Gaeltacht districts.
English in Kerry and west Cork.
Brittonic held Devon until about 700 and Cornwall far longer. The last native speakers of Cornish died in the 18th century.
The Romance speech of Christians, and many Muslims, under Muslim rule. Often called Mozarabic.
Romance speech replaced Greek and Arabic in Sicily and southern Calabria after the Norman conquest.
Shetland before the Norse. The language is assumed to be that of the Picts and is not recorded.
Scots replaced Norn in Shetland between the 15th and 18th centuries.
English in the west Highlands. Gaelic is still spoken in the Hebrides.
English of Northumberland and the Borders.
Irish was still the main language of most of Ulster through the plantation of the 17th century.
Man before the 6th century. Brittonic or Irish, and not recorded.
Gaelic lasted under the Norse kings of Man and became Manx.
Corsican is close to Tuscan. French is now the majority language.
Provencal in the south and Franco-Provencal in Savoy, both giving way to French in the 19th century.
The far south-west, where the Tartessian inscriptions were cut centuries earlier. The language under Rome is not known.
Romance speech under Muslim rule, before the Catalan settlement of the 13th century.
Greek and Latin shared Sicily under Rome and Byzantium, with Arabic beside them from the 9th century.
Belgic Gaulish in what is now Hainaut.
The Romance speech of southern Belgium.
Frisian along the coast and around the later Zuiderzee.
Low German in Holstein.
Slavic speech reached the Adriatic by the 7th century. Dalmatian Romance lasted in the towns until the 19th century.
Ukrainian of Galicia.
Slavic speech on the upper Tisza.
Russian has been the majority language of Crimea since the deportation of the Crimean Tatars in 1944. Sovereignty over Crimea is disputed.
Dacian peoples of the northern Carpathians, known as the Costoboci a little later.
The Aleutian chain. Archaeology shows the same sea-hunting people here for several thousand years. Most Unangan now speak English.
Western Aleutians, thinly peopled and almost emptied by removals in the 1940s.
South-west Alaska. Projected back from the time of contact through the Norton tradition.
Kodiak and the Gulf of Alaska coast. Projected back from the time of contact.
Bering Strait and north-west Alaska. The Old Bering Sea, Birnirk and Thule cultures are taken to be ancestral Inuit.
The north slope of Alaska, thinly peopled. Before about 900 the language is assumed.
Thule Inuit moved east along the coast about 1200.
Central Canadian Arctic. Thinly peopled coast and tundra.
Baffin Island and Foxe Basin.
The high Arctic islands. Very thinly peopled and largely abandoned in the cold centuries after 1500.
Northern Quebec.
The Labrador coast.
West Greenland. Inuit crossed from Ellesmere Island about 1200 to 1300. Greenlandic is the majority language today.
South Greenland, reached as the Norse settlements failed.
East Greenland and the ice cap. A thin wash. The ice itself is empty.
North Greenland and the ice cap. A thin wash. The far north was abandoned for long periods.
The Dorset culture, the Tuniit of Inuit tradition. Their language is unknown. Thinly peopled.
The western Canadian Arctic was at the edge of the Dorset world and very thinly peopled. Language unknown.
Baffin Island and Foxe Basin, the Dorset heartland. Language unknown.
The high Arctic islands, peopled only at times. Language unknown.
Northern Quebec and Labrador, where Dorset sites last longest. Language unknown.
Greenland. A thin wash only: most of Greenland seems to have stood empty between about 1 and 700, and the ice cap always.
The Eastern Settlement. The landing is dated from sagas written two centuries later and from archaeology.
The Eastern Settlement, with a bishop at Gardar from the 1120s. The last written record is of a wedding at Hvalsey in 1408.
The Western Settlement.
The Western Settlement, reported deserted about 1350. Radiocarbon dates suggest some people stayed until about 1400.
Interior Alaska. Linguists place the Athabaskan homeland in interior Alaska, Yukon and northern British Columbia. Thinly peopled forest.
Yukon. Projected back from the time of contact.
The Mackenzie valley. Projected back from the time of contact.
The edge of the barren lands, thinly peopled. The Taltheilei tradition is taken to be ancestral Dene.
The barren lands west of Hudson Bay, very thinly peopled. Inuit have held the coast since about 1700.
Northern Alberta and Saskatchewan. Projected back from the time of contact.
Interior British Columbia. Projected back from the time of contact.
The Alaska panhandle. Projected back from the time of contact. Tlingit is a distant relative of Athabaskan.
Haida, Tsimshian and their neighbours. Archaeology shows long continuity on this coast. Projected back from the time of contact.
Wakashan speakers of Vancouver Island and the facing coast. Projected back from the time of contact.
Coast Salish. Projected back from the time of contact.
Interior Salish of the plateau. Projected back from the time of contact.
Kalispel, Flathead Salish and the Ktunaxa, whose language is an isolate. Projected back from the time of contact.
California held some twenty language families. Projected back from the time of contact.
Chumash and the Takic speakers of southern California. Projected back from the time of contact.
Chinookan, Sahaptian and the small families of Oregon. Projected back from the time of contact.
Sahaptian speakers of the Columbia Plateau. Projected back from the time of contact.
The northern Great Basin before the Numic spread. Thinly peopled and the languages are unknown. This wash is a guess.
Linguists place the Numic homeland near Death Valley. Desert, thinly peopled.
Numic speakers spread across the Great Basin after about 1000. The date is debated.
Ute country. Projected back from the time of contact.
Shoshone of the Snake River and Wyoming.
The Comanche left the Shoshone, took to horses and held the southern Plains from about 1720.
Comanche bands on their way south along the mountain front.
Utah before the Numic spread, the land of the Fremont culture. The language is unknown. Kiowa-Tanoan is one guess.
Bison hunters of the northern High Plains. Languages unknown. Kiowa tradition places their own origin near the Yellowstone.
The central High Plains, thinly peopled. Languages unknown.
The southern High Plains, thinly peopled. Languages unknown.
Athabaskan speakers came south along the Plains between about 1200 and 1500. The route and date are debated.
Navajo country. Spanish writers name the Navajo from the 1620s. Navajo is still widely spoken here.
Apache bands of New Mexico and west Texas.
Western and Chiricahua Apache, on both sides of the present border.
Lipan Apache, pushed south by the Comanche.
Western Apache reservations.
The Ancestral Pueblo country. Tanoan, Keresan and Zuni are assumed from where their speakers live now.
The Rio Grande pueblos, described by the Coronado expedition in 1540.
Zuni and Hopi before the first Spanish visit.
Zuni and Hopi. Hopi is a Uto-Aztecan language.
The Mogollon highlands. The language is unknown and assumed to be like that of the later pueblos.
The lower Colorado River. Projected back from the time of contact.
Northern Baja California. Projected back from the time of contact.
Southern Baja California, thinly peopled. Cochimi was related to Yuman. Guaycura and Pericu are unclassified.
The Sonoran desert. O'odham speech is assumed for the Hohokam farmers before 1450.
Yaqui, Mayo and Opata. Projected back from the time of contact.
The Sierra Madre. Rarámuri is still spoken here.
The Chihuahua desert, thinly peopled. The Concho and their neighbours are poorly recorded.
Tepehuan, Cora, Huichol and Zacatec. Projected back from the time of contact.
Cora and Wixárika (Huichol) country.
Hunters of south Texas and north-east Mexico. Many small languages, mostly unrecorded. Projected back from the time of contact.
Tamaulipas. Poorly recorded languages. Projected back from the time of contact.
Karankawa, Tonkawa and Atakapa of the Texas coast. Projected back from the time of contact.
Natchez, Tunica and Chitimacha on the lower Mississippi. Projected back from the time of contact.
The central Mississippi valley. The languages of its towns are mostly unknown. Tunica is one candidate.
Timucua, Calusa and the other peoples of Florida, recorded by Spanish missions and gone by the 1760s.
The upper Great Lakes, near where many linguists place the Algonquian homeland. Projected back from the time of contact.
Ojibwe country around Lake Superior.
Cree of the forest around James Bay, thinly peopled. Cree is still spoken across the north.
Innu and Naskapi of Quebec and Labrador, thinly peopled. Projected back from the time of contact.
Cree of the forest west of Hudson Bay, thinly peopled. Projected back from the time of contact.
Mi'kmaq and Wabanaki country. Projected back from the time of contact.
Eastern Algonquian of the Atlantic coast. It reached the coast at an uncertain date, perhaps before 500.
Southern New England. Projected back from the time of contact.
Illinois, Miami and Shawnee country. For the centuries of the Hopewell mounds the language is unknown.
The northern Plains. Blackfoot, Gros Ventre and later Plains Cree. Projected back from the time of contact.
Blackfoot country. The language has been long apart from its relatives, which suggests a long stay in the west.
Cree moved west with the fur trade.
Cheyenne and Arapaho, who moved from the woodland edge onto the Plains.
Newfoundland. The Beothuk language is known from a few word lists and may or may not be Algonquian.
The lower Great Lakes. Most archaeologists see Iroquoian speakers here from at least 1000, and many from much earlier.
The St Lawrence Iroquoians before Cartier, known from archaeology.
The St Lawrence Iroquoians, met by Cartier in 1535 and gone by 1600.
Cherokee of the southern Appalachians. Projected back from the time of contact.
Tuscarora and their neighbours.
The Cherokee Nation after removal.
Dakota, Ho-Chunk and Ioway of the upper Mississippi. Projected back from the time of contact.
The Red River valley. Projected back from the time of contact.
The Ohio valley, where some linguists place the Siouan homeland. The languages of its mound builders are unknown.
Catawba, Tutelo and their neighbours of the Piedmont.
Farming villages of the Missouri valley.
Mandan and Hidatsa earth-lodge villages.
Osage, Quapaw and their relatives.
The Crow left the Hidatsa and moved up the Yellowstone.
Assiniboine (Nakoda).
The Lakota crossed the Missouri with horses in the later 18th century.
Lakota and Dakota reservations.
The South-east. Projected back from the time of contact, when de Soto's men met Muskogean-speaking chiefdoms.
Seminole in Florida.
The removed nations in the Indian Territory.
Caddo country. Archaeology shows continuity here from about 800.
Wichita and Pawnee of the central Plains. Projected back from the time of contact.
The Arikara moved up the Missouri.
Before Nahuatl reached the central valleys its speakers lived somewhere to the north-west. The position is a guess.
Nahuatl reached central Mexico between about 500 and 900. Whether any of Teotihuacan spoke it is debated.
The Nahua heartland at its widest.
Nahua of the west. Projected back from the time of contact.
The Pipil, Nahua who moved to El Salvador.
The Huasteca and the Sierra of Puebla, where Nahuatl is still widely spoken.
Nahuatl of Guerrero.
Oaxaca. Zapotec and Mixtec have been spoken here since long before 1 CE, and still are.
Otomi, Mazahua and Matlatzinca of the central highlands, there before Nahuatl.
Otomi country.
The dry north, land of hunters the Nahua called Chichimeca. Pame is Oto-Manguean. Other languages here are unknown.
Tlapanec and the lost languages of Guerrero. Projected back from the time of contact.
Chorotega (Mangue), who moved south from Mexico.
The isthmus of Tehuantepec, the old Olmec country. A few early inscriptions here seem to be in a Zoquean language.
Central Veracruz. Projected back from the time of contact.
Totonac country.
Michoacan. Purépecha has no known relatives. Projected back from the time of contact.
The lowlands, where inscriptions in a Ch'olan Mayan language run from before 1 CE to about 900. Yucatec Maya is still widely spoken.
The Guatemalan highlands, near where linguists place the Mayan homeland.
Tzotzil and Tzeltal of Chiapas.
Ch'orti' country around Copan.
Huastec, a Mayan language far to the north-west of the others.
Lenca and Xinca. Projected back from the time of contact.
Tol and Pech of northern Honduras. Projected back from the time of contact.
Misumalpan languages. Miskito is still the main language of the Caribbean shore.
Costa Rica and western Panama, where linguists place the Chibchan homeland.
Rama and Guatuso. Projected back from the time of contact.
Panama. The language of the Cueva chiefdoms met by Balboa is poorly recorded.
Bribri, Cabecar and Ngabe country.
Guna and Embera of eastern Panama. Embera is a Choco language.
The Muisca highlands. Muisca was written down by missionaries and died out in the 18th century.
The Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta, Tairona country, where Kogi and Ika are still spoken.
U'wa, Bari and the peoples of the Venezuelan Andes, whose Timote language was not Chibchan.
The Caribbean lowlands of Colombia. The Zenu language is unknown and Chibchan is an assumption.
Western Cuba. Foragers known only from archaeology. Their language is unknown.
Central Cuba. Foragers known only from archaeology. Their language is unknown.
Eastern Cuba. Foragers known only from archaeology. Their language is unknown.
Hispaniola before the pottery-making farmers spread west. Language unknown.
The far west of Cuba, where Spanish writers place the Guanahatabey. Whether they were a separate people is disputed.
Puerto Rico and eastern Hispaniola. Saladoid potters from the Orinoco, taken to be Arawakan speakers, arrived a few centuries before 1 CE.
The Lesser Antilles. The Kalinago language was Arawakan with a Carib vocabulary used by men.
Kalinago and Garifuna on Dominica and St Vincent.
Trinidad, shared by Arawakan and Cariban speakers.
