Thinly peopled desert. Tuareg of the Air mountains. Tradition says Hausa speakers lived in Air before them.
Brought by the Banu Hassan, Arab nomads who moved south through the western Sahara from about 1400.
The Arabic of Mauritania. Thinly peopled desert outside the south.
Soninke, the language of Ghana. Stone-built villages at Dhar Tichitt are older than 1 CE.
The Manding heartland on the upper Niger: Malinke and Bambara.
Bozo and Bambara on the middle Niger around Jenne.
Mandinka, carried west to the Gambia by the Mali empire.
Mende, Kpelle, Loma and Vai. Portuguese writers record invaders from inland, the Mane, about 1545.
Dyula traders and the south-eastern Mande languages.
Wolof and Serer in Senegambia. Written of by Arab authors from the 11th century and by the Portuguese from the 1440s.
Balanta, Baga, Landuma and other languages of the rivers of Guinea.
Temne, Bullom, Kissi and Gola.
Fula took shape in the Senegal valley. The early date is a guess.
Fula herders in Massina, the inland delta of the Niger.
Futa Jallon, settled by Fula between the 15th and 17th centuries.
Liptako and northern Burkina Faso.
Adamawa, where Fula became the common language after the jihad of 1809.
The Niger bend around Gao. The town is named by Arab writers from the 9th century.
Upstream to Timbuktu and Jenne.
Zarma and Dendi, downstream from Gao.
Moore, Gurma, Dagbani and their relatives in the Volta basin. Dates before 1400 rest on reconstruction.
Senufo languages.
Kru, Grebo, Bete and Dida. Kru is its own branch of Niger-Congo and is keyed here with its eastern neighbours for want of a closer family.
Twi, Fante and Ga, and Baule and Anyi in the west from the 18th century.
The Gbe languages between the Volta and the Weme.
Yoruba and Igala. Towns such as Ife are known from about 900.
Igbo and Edo, with Ijo in the delta and Efik and Ibibio on the Cross River, which are other families.
Many small Benue-Congo languages, with Nupe, Idoma, Jukun and Tiv. The Nok culture lay in this zone.
Chadic languages. When Hausa itself spread west across this plain is debated.
Hausa. The walled towns date from about 1000 to 1200.
Kebbi, Zamfara and Gobir.
Kotoko, Musgu, Mafa and other Chadic languages south of Lake Chad.
Eastern Chadic languages of the Guera hills.
Thinly peopled desert. Teda and Daza of Tibesti and Borkou, called Tubu by their neighbours.
Kanembu, north and east of Lake Chad.
Kanuri in Bornu, where the rulers of Kanem moved in the 14th century.
Desert with almost no settled people. Zaghawa of Ennedi and northern Darfur, named by Arab writers from the 9th century, and nomads who crossed the sands to the north.
Arab cattle nomads reached the Chad basin from the Nile by about 1400. Their Arabic became the common language of the country.
Fur and Masalit around Jebel Marra. Unwritten before the 19th century.
Maba and its relatives in Wadai.
Daju and other small languages between Darfur and the Nuba Mountains.
Sara and Bagirmi on the Chari and Logone.
Madi, Lugbara, Mangbetu and Lendu, from the Uele to the Nile.
Mumuye, Chamba, Mbum and other Adamawa languages.
Gbaya.
Banda, Ngbandi and Sango.
Ubangi languages. Zande spread east over this ground in the 18th and 19th centuries.
Ndogo, Kresh and other small languages of western Bahr el Ghazal, some of them not Ubangi.
The written language of Kush. Its family is not settled. Many scholars now place it near Nubian.
The Butana and the Blue Nile. What was spoken beyond the towns is not known.
Nubian speakers west of the Nile, inferred from the Hill Nubian, Midob and Birgid languages and from the Noba named by Ezana.
Nubian on the Nile after Kush. Old Nubian was written from the 8th to the 15th century.
The kingdom of Alwa. Its Nubian is barely recorded.
Nobiin and Dongolawi, still spoken along the river.
Hill Nubian in the northern Nuba Mountains.
Dozens of small languages of several families, some Nilo-Saharan and some not.
Thinly peopled hills. The Beja are the Blemmyes of Roman writers and the Buja of Arab ones.
Arab nomads moved up the Nile as Makuria broke down in the 14th century. Ibn Khaldun describes it. How fast Arabic replaced Nubian is debated, and some scholars place the shift under the Funj.
The Gezira and Butana under the Funj.
Kordofan.
Baggara cattle nomads south of Darfur.
Dinka, Nuer and Shilluk in the Sudd. The homeland of the family by reconstruction.
Bari, Lotuko, Karimojong and Teso, with small Surmic and Kuliak languages.
Southern Nilotic, the ancestor of Kalenjin and Datooga, in the western highlands of Kenya by reconstruction.
Datooga and other Southern Nilotic herders held these plains before the Maasai.
Luo speakers, the Acholi, Lango and Alur, moved south from the Sudd from about 1400 by tradition.
Luo of the Kenyan lake shore.
Maa, the language of the Maasai, spread down the Rift Valley in the 17th and 18th centuries.
Turkana.
Gumuz, Berta and Koman languages along the escarpment.
Kunama and Nara. Aksumite inscriptions name peoples here.
Ge'ez, written at Aksum, and its successors Tigrinya and Tigre.
Amharic spread south over Agaw ground as the kingdom moved south. The start date is a guess.
Shewa, with Gurage, an older southern relative of Amharic.
Harari and Argobba, the Semitic speech of the Muslim towns of the east.
The Cushitic language of the highlands before Semitic speech spread. Cosmas names the Agaw.
Awngi and other remnants. Bilen in Eritrea and Qemant near Gondar are others.
The Oromo homeland in the southern highlands, by reconstruction and tradition.
From the 1520s the Oromo spread north. Bahrey described the movement in 1593.
Wellega and the Gibe states.
Borana and Orma in northern Kenya. Thinly peopled.
Eastern Cushitic speech ancestral to Somali. The Periplus calls the coast people Barbaroi. When Somali spread over the Horn is debated.
The Jubba and Shabelle, held by many scholars to be where Somali took shape.
Somali. Arab geographers describe Zeila, Berbera and Mogadishu.
Southern Somalia. Ibn Battuta visited Mogadishu about 1331.
The Harar plateau before the Oromo. Tradition names a vanished people, the Harla. Their speech is not known and Eastern Cushitic is a guess.
Thinly peopled. Rendille, Aweer and other relatives of Somali, and Somali itself in the north-east from the 19th century.
Thinly peopled desert. The Afar are the Dankal of Arab writers from the 13th century.
Highland East Cushitic languages of the Rift lakes.
Wolaytta, Kafa, Gamo and others in the south-west. Unwritten before the 19th century.
Near the Bantu homeland on the Nigeria and Cameroon border. Fang, Duala, Basaa and the Grassfields languages today.
Gabon and the lower Congo, reached before 1 CE by the evidence of pottery and iron.
The Congo forest, settled along the rivers. Mongo and Lingala today. Thinly peopled away from the rivers.
The Lualaba forest. Thinly peopled, and the date farmers arrived is a guess.
The savanna south of the forest. Kongo, Kimbundu and Pende today.
The Angolan plateau. Umbundu and Nyaneka today. The date is a guess.
Chokwe, Luvale, Ngangela and Lozi country on the upper Zambezi.
Katanga. Ironworking farmers lived in the Upemba basin by about 500. Luba and Lunda today.
Ovambo and Kavango languages. They may have arrived some centuries earlier.
Herero, in central Namibia by the 18th century.
The Great Lakes, where Urewe pottery and iron smelting date from before 1 CE. Rwanda, Rundi, Ganda and Haya today.
The north and east shores of Lake Victoria. Ganda, Soga and Luhya today.
Kwale pottery marks farmers in the coastal hills from about 200. Mijikenda, Chaga and Shambaa today.
Western Tanzania. Ha, Nyamwezi and Fipa today. The date is a guess.
Central Tanzania. Sukuma, Gogo and Nyaturu today. The date is a guess.
Southern Tanzania. Hehe, Makonde and Nyakyusa today.
Kikuyu, Kamba and Meru around Mount Kenya.
The Lamu islands, where Swahili took shape. Shanga had a mosque by about 800.
Mombasa, Pemba and Zanzibar. Al-Masudi sailed to this coast in 916.
Kilwa and Mafia.
Swahili is now the common language of Tanzania, beside the home languages.
Nkope and Kalambo pottery marks farmers from about 300. Bemba, Chewa and Tumbuka today.
Makua, Yao and Makonde. The date is a guess.
The Kalundu tradition of southern Zambia. Tonga and Ila today.
The lower Zambezi. Sena and Nyungwe today.
Gokomere and Ziwa pottery marks farmers on the plateau from about 300. Shona from about 900.
Matola pottery on the coastal plain from about 200. Tsonga and Chopi today.
Farming villages north of the Vaal from about 400. Northern Sotho, Venda and Ndebele today.
Natal, farmed from about 400. Zulu today.
Farmers reached the Kei River by about 700. Xhosa today.
Cattle-keeping villages of eastern Botswana, the Toutswe tradition.
Tswana, in stone-walled towns west of the Limpopo.
Sotho speakers settled the grassland south of the Vaal from about 1400.
Tswana is the common language of Botswana. The Kalahari is thinly peopled.
Khoekhoe herders. Sheep bones and pottery place herding at the Cape about 2000 years ago. That the first herders spoke Khoekhoe is likely but not proven.
Nama, along the Orange River and in Namaqualand. Thinly peopled.
Thinly peopled. Damara and Hai//om speak Khoekhoe. How long they have done so is not known.
Khwe, Naro, Shua and other Khoe languages around the Okavango and Makgadikgadi.
The Kalahari. Ju and Taa languages. Thinly peopled.
Foragers of the grassland and the Drakensberg, known from rock paintings. Farmers took the lowlands after about 400.
San of the Maloti and Drakensberg, the last painters.
The Karoo. /Xam, recorded in the 1870s as it died out.
Foragers before the farmers came. Their languages are unrecorded. Khoe and San speech is assumed from what survives further west.
Foragers of northern Namibia and southern Angola. !Xun and the extinct Kwadi are what remains.
Foragers of the upper Zambezi. Khwe and !Xun are still spoken in the south of this ground.
!Xun and Hai//om country around Etosha.
Thinly peopled. Later Stone Age foragers lived here before Bantu-speaking farmers came. Nothing is known of their languages.
Thinly peopled. Foragers of the Rovuma country. Their languages are unknown.
Thinly peopled. Foragers of the southern savanna before the farmers. Their languages are unknown.
Foragers of the Tanzanian interior before farming. Their languages are unknown. Hadza and Sandawe are taken to be what is left.
Hadza near Lake Eyasi and Sandawe to the south. Neither has proven relatives.
Herders of the Rift highlands, known from the Pastoral Neolithic sites and from words borrowed into later languages.
Iraqw and its relatives around Mbulu, before any written record of them.
Iraqw and its relatives around Mbulu, recorded from the German period.
Dutch at the Cape from 1652, spoken by settlers, slaves and Khoekhoe, and becoming Afrikaans.
The western Cape and the Karoo.
The Orange River frontier, carried by Griqua, Oorlam and trekking farmers.
British settlers of 1820 in the eastern Cape.
Durban and the Natal coast.
Johannesburg, after gold was found in 1886.
Cape Verde had no people before Portuguese settlement began in 1462. Its creole grew from Portuguese and West African languages.
Sao Tome and Principe were empty until Portugal settled them from the 1480s.
Kingdom of the middle Nile, with its capital at Meroe. Its language is written but little understood. It ended about 350.
Named west of the Nile by Greek writers and by Ezana of Aksum, who fought them about 350. Taken to be Nubian speakers.
The Blemmyes of Roman writers, who raided Upper Egypt.
The Buja of Arab writers. Bedawiyet is their name for their language.
Northern Nubian kingdom with its capital at Faras. Christian from the 540s and joined to Makuria in the 7th century, probably before 652.
Kingdom of Old Dongola. It held off the Arabs in 652 and kept a treaty with Egypt for six centuries.
A remnant in Lower Nubia after Dongola was given up, with its court at Gebel Adda. Its last known king reigned in the 1480s.
Also Alodia, the southern Nubian kingdom with its capital at Soba, first named in 569 and Christian from 580. Arab writers describe it in the 10th century.
Its last two centuries are barely recorded. Soba fell about 1500, and sources disagree on whether to Arabs or to the Funj.
Muslim kingdom of Sennar. Where the Funj came from is disputed. Arabic was the language of the court. Egypt conquered it in 1821.
Nobiin and Dongolawi speakers of the river. Many were moved when the Aswan dam flooded their land in the 1960s.
The Periplus names the city of the Aksumites and its port, Adulis.
At its height. Ezana took up Christianity about 340 and Kaleb sent an army to Yemen about 525.
In decline after it lost the Red Sea trade. The kings moved south.
The older people of the northern highlands, with whom Aksumite kings record wars. Awi and other Agaw keep the language today and are carried by the wash after 1300.
Christian dynasty of Agaw origin, builders of the rock churches of Lalibela. Its start date is uncertain.
The Solomonic kings, who claimed descent from Aksum and from Solomon. Abyssinia to outsiders.
Reduced by the war with Adal and by the Oromo expansion, with a capital at Gondar from 1636.
Reunited under Tewodros and doubled in size by Menelik, who beat Italy at Adwa in 1896.
Speakers of Amharic, the language of the court from 1270. Before 1900 the entry Ethiopia stands for them.
The people of the old Aksumite heartland in the poorly recorded centuries after Aksum.
Tigrinya speakers of Tigray and highland Eritrea, on the ground of Aksum.
The Periplus lists market towns of the Barbaroi along this coast. That they spoke early Somali is an inference.
Arab writers describe the towns of this coast from the 10th century and call its people Berbers.
Soomaali. Ibn Battuta visited Zeila and Mogadishu about 1331 and the name Somali appears in an Ethiopian hymn of the early 15th century.
Herders of the southern highlands, organised by the gada age system.
After 1522 the Oromo spread over much of Ethiopia. Older writers call them Galla, a name they reject.
Herders of the Danakil desert. Dankal in Arabic.

Muslim sultanate of the Walashma, whose people spoke Ethiopian Semitic and Cushitic languages and wrote Arabic, so the key is a guess. Its last sultan died at Zeila in 1403 or 1415, and sources disagree on which.
Successor of Ifat, based at Harar from 1520. Under Ahmad Gran it overran Ethiopia between 1529 and 1543. Somali, Afar and Harari served it.
Somali sultanate of the Shabelle valley, known mainly from tradition.
A modern name. Herders of the Rift known from archaeology and from loanwords. The Iraqw of Tanzania are their heirs.
Jieng in their own language, cattle keepers of the Sudd, first written of in the 19th century. The Ngok Dinka live in Abyei, whose sovereignty is disputed between Sudan and South Sudan.
Acholi, Lango and Alur, Luo speakers who moved south from the Sudd.
Joluo of the Kenyan lake shore.
Maa-speaking herders who took the Rift grasslands in the 17th and 18th centuries.
Described by missionaries and travellers from the 1840s.
Jenne-jeno and its neighbours, towns of rice farmers, smiths and traders from before 1 CE. Known from excavation only.
Wagadu in Soninke tradition. When the kingdom began is not known.
The land of gold to Arab writers from about 800. They name it but do not yet describe it.
Al-Yaqubi describes the kingdom in the late 9th century and al-Bakri its capital in 1068.
Whether the Almoravids conquered it in 1076 is disputed. The Sosso took it about 1203 and Mali by about 1240.
Kingdom on the lower Senegal. Its history before the 11th century rests on tradition.
Its king War Jabi took up Islam in the 1030s, as al-Bakri reports. Mali conquered it about 1285.
The town grew from the 8th century. Al-Khwarizmi names it before 850.
Kawkaw to Arab writers, the greatest realm of the Sudan to al-Yaqubi about 872. It was under Mali from about 1300 to the early 15th century.
Founded by Sunjata Keita by tradition. Ibn Khaldun gives a king list.
From the Atlantic to Gao. Mansa Musa went to Mecca in 1324 and Ibn Battuta visited in 1352.
Shrunk back to the Manding heartland. It failed to take Jenne in 1599 and broke up after its last mansa died about 1610.
Built by Sunni Ali and Askia Muhammad from Gao. A Moroccan army with guns broke it at Tondibi in 1591.

Ouagadougou, Yatenga and their sister kingdoms, Moose in their own language, whose horsemen raided Timbuktu and Walata in the 15th century. Founding dates from tradition range from the 11th to the 15th century.
European travellers reached Ouagadougou in the 1880s. France took it in 1896.
The Jolof empire, founded by Ndiadiane Ndiaye by tradition, about the middle of the 14th century.
Described by Cadamosto, who sailed here in 1455. It broke up after the battle of Danki in 1549.
Kayor, Waalo, Baol and Jolof after the empire broke up.
Bambara kingdom on the Niger, built by Biton Kulibali from about 1712.
Visited by Mungo Park in 1796. Umar Tal took it in 1861.
Veiled Berber nomads of the western desert before Arab writers describe them.
Veiled Berber (Amazigh) nomads, the Lamtuna, Guddala and Massufa, named by al-Yaqubi and described by al-Bakri. The Almoravid movement began among them in the 1040s.

Hassaniya-speaking nomads of Arab and Berber descent, under the emirates of Trarza, Brakna and Adrar until the French conquest. Their country runs north into Western Sahara, whose sovereignty is disputed.
Berber nomads around Tadmakka, a trading town of the Adrar des Ifoghas.
Kel Tamasheq, speakers of Tamasheq, in their own language, and Tuareg to outsiders. Al-Bakri describes Tadmakka in 1068 and Ibn Battuta crossed their country in 1353.
Tuareg of Air, with a sultan at Agadez from the 15th century.
Fulbe in their own language, Fulani in Hausa, Peul in French. Cattle herders who began on the Senegal.
Fula of Massina.
Fula herders in the Futa Jallon highlands before the jihad.
Fula of Futa Jallon.
Fula herders and clerics reached Hausaland by the 15th century and Bagirmi by the 16th, a minority among Hausa and others. Evidence for the move east is thin.
Walled towns and terracotta figures south of Lake Chad. Sao is the name later tradition gives their builders, taken to be Chadic speakers.
Founded about 700 by later reckoning, before any writer names it.
Named by al-Yaqubi in 872. Its Sayfawa kings took up Islam in the 11th century and left for Bornu about 1380.
The Sayfawa kingdom west of Lake Chad, strongest under Idris Alooma about 1600. Rabih conquered it in 1893.
People of Tibesti. Tubu, the name others use, means rock people.
Kano, Katsina, Zazzau, Gobir and others. Early reigns rest on the Kano Chronicle, which is late.
Walled trading cities, never one state. Leo Africanus describes them about 1510.
Hausa is now the most widely spoken language of the Sahel.
Maba-speaking sultanate, founded by Abd al-Karim about 1635 by tradition.
Described by al-Tunisi, who lived there about 1810, and by Nachtigal. France took its capital in 1909 and ended the sultanate in 1912.
The Keira sultans of the Fur, in power from about the middle of the 17th century.
Described by Browne, who lived there from 1793, when its capital was newly at al-Fashir. Conquered for Egypt in 1874.
Restored by Ali Dinar in 1898 and annexed to the Sudan in 1916.
Fula clerics took power in the highlands from 1725, with a capital at Timbo.
Founded by Usman dan Fodio's jihad of 1804, which had taken the Hausa cities by 1808. Fula emirs ruled from Sokoto to Adamawa.
The state of Seku Amadu, with its capital at Hamdullahi.
Built by al-Hajj Umar Tal, who took Segu in 1861 and Massina in 1862. France conquered it by 1893.
Farmers and ironworkers known for terracotta sculpture, from before 500 BCE to the early centuries CE. Their language is unknown.
Cast bronzes and a rich burial of the 9th or 10th century, in what is now Igbo country.
Village communities without kings, with a ritual centre at Nri.
Named in European records of the slave trade and by Olaudah Equiano in 1789.
The first Yoruba city by tradition. Its brass and terracotta heads date from about 1100 to 1400.
Kingdom of the Edo. Its king list reaches back to about 1200.
Portuguese envoys reached the city in 1485. A British force sacked it in 1897.
Yoruba kingdom of the northern savanna. Early dates are from tradition.
Tradition has the kings return to Oyo-Ile about 1610 after an exile forced by Nupe.
A cavalry empire that reached the coast and took tribute from Dahomey, known to European traders there from about 1700. Its capital was destroyed about 1835.
After Oyo, Ibadan and other cities fought for its place. The shared name Yoruba came into wide use in the 19th century.
The first Akan state by tradition, on the gold road north to Jenne.
Osei Tutu united the Akan around Kumasi and beat Denkyira in 1701.
At its widest most of modern Ghana. Also written Ashanti. Britain occupied Kumasi in 1896.
Asante, Fante and other speakers of Twi.
Fon kingdom of Abomey, founded in the early 17th century by tradition.
It took the coastal kingdoms of Allada and Whydah in the 1720s, when European traders first describe it. France conquered it in 1894.
Portuguese sailors reached this coast in the 1460s and called its peoples Sapes.
Named by Portuguese writers from the first years of the 16th century.
Often linked with the Mane invaders of the 1540s. The link is an inference.
A modern label, not a people's name. Villages with pottery, oil palm and iron along the rivers of the forest.
Pottery and iron smelting around Lake Victoria from about 500 BCE. Taken to mark the first Bantu speakers in East Africa.
Pottery of the hills behind the Kenya and Tanzania coast, related to Urewe.
Early farming villages around Lake Malawi.
Early farming villages of southern and western Zambia. Whether it came from the west or the east is debated.
The first farmers of the Zimbabwe plateau.
The first farmers of the south-east coast, from Maputo Bay to Natal, related to Kwale.
The empire of the Chwezi in court tradition. The earthworks at Bigo and Ntusi are of this age. How much of the story is history is disputed.
Kingdom of the Bito dynasty, of Luo origin by tradition.
Visited by Speke in 1862. Uganda abolished its kingdoms in 1967.
A small kingdom on the lake shore that grew at Bunyoro's cost from about 1700.
The strongest lake kingdom when Speke arrived in 1862.
Kingdom of the Nyiginya dynasty, ended in 1961. Scholars date its founding between the 14th and 17th centuries.
Founded about 1390 by tradition, with its capital at Mbanza Kongo.
Portuguese ships arrived in 1483 and the king was baptised in 1491. Its kings wrote in Portuguese.
Broken by defeat at Mbwila in 1665 and by civil war. The title lasted until 1914.
Bakongo, on both banks of the lower Congo in Angola, DR Congo and the Republic of the Congo.
Mbundu kingdom whose ruler's title, ngola, named Angola.
A Portuguese mission reached its court in 1520. Queen Njinga fought Portugal from Matamba until 1663.
Kingdom between the Kasai and Sankuru, founded by Shyaam by tradition.
Graves with copper and fine pottery in the Upemba basin, the Kisalian phase. On the ground of the later Luba.
Kingdom of the upper Lualaba, whose ideas of kingship spread widely. Scholars date its founding anywhere from before 1500 to the 18th century.
Baluba of Katanga and Kasai, among the largest peoples of DR Congo.
The realm of the Mwant Yav, with tributaries from the Kwango to the Luapula.
Chewa-speaking kingdoms south of the lake, founded by the Phiri clan by tradition.
First described by Gaspar Bocarro, who crossed it in 1616. Malawi takes its name from it.
The Periplus names the coast Azania and its last market Rhapta, which has not been found. What its people spoke is not known.
The Lamu islands, with early mosques at Shanga. Pate and Lamu were later city states.
The Zanj of Arab writers. Al-Masudi sailed to this coast in 916, but the towns of this time are placed by archaeology.
Waswahili, people of the coast. Ibn Battuta visited Mombasa and Kilwa about 1331 and calls the coast the Sawahil.
The Kilwa Chronicle puts its founding in the 10th century and archaeology somewhat later.
Sultanate that held the gold trade of Sofala. Ibn Battuta visited about 1331 and Portugal sacked it in 1505.
The southern port of the gold trade. Arab writers from al-Masudi on use the name for a whole coast, and the town is first placed by the Portuguese, who built a fort there in 1505.
Oman took the coast from Portugal by 1698 and its sultan moved to Zanzibar about 1840. Britain made it a protectorate in 1890.
A capital on the Limpopo, rich in gold, at the site called K2 and from about 1220 on Mapungubwe hill. Known from excavation only, and its people are taken to be early Shona speakers.
The largest stone-built town south of the Sahara. No writing of its own time names it.
Shona kingdom of the northern plateau, founded in the 15th century by tradition.
Portuguese letters name it from 1506 and write Monomotapa.
A client of Portugal after 1629 and much reduced.
Kingdom of the south-west plateau with its stone capital at Khami.
Changamire Dombo took Butua about 1683 and drove the Portuguese off the plateau in the 1690s. Nguni armies broke the state in the 1830s.
The shared name is of the 19th century. Zezuru, Karanga, Manyika and others.
Survivors of Portuguese shipwrecks describe cattle-keeping farmers on this coast from the 1550s.
AmaXhosa. They fought nine frontier wars with the Cape Colony between 1779 and 1879.
Small chiefdoms, and by 1800 the Mthethwa and Ndwandwe confederacies.
The kingdom Shaka built from 1816. Britain broke it in 1879.
AmaZulu, the largest language community of South Africa.
Basotho. Moshoeshoe gathered refugees on Thaba Bosiu in the 1820s. Lesotho is their state.
Chiefdoms with large stone-walled towns.
Batswana. Travellers reached the town of Dithakong in 1801.
Mzilikazi left Shaka about 1822 and ruled the highveld until the Boers drove him north.
AmaNdebele of Matabeleland. Their kingdom lasted until 1893.
Nguni state founded by Soshangane over Tsonga and Shona country. Portugal defeated Ngungunyane in 1895.
Nguni bands under Zwangendaba crossed the Zambezi in 1835 and settled from Malawi to southern Tanzania.
Aawambo. Farming kingdoms of the Cuvelai floodplain.
Ovaherero, cattle herders who came south from the Kunene. Accounts of when they arrived range from the 15th to the 18th century.
Most were killed or driven out by German forces between 1904 and 1908.
Agikuyu. Farmers of the ridges south of Mount Kenya.
The largest people of northern Mozambique, behind the Portuguese post on Mozambique Island.
Named by Portuguese writers from about 1600.
Foragers of the Ituri forest. Their own language is lost.
Described by Schweinfurth and Stanley. They speak the Bantu and Central Sudanic languages of their neighbours.
Foragers of the western forest. Aka speak a Bantu language and Baka an Ubangi one. Their older languages are lost.
Herders known from sheep bones and pottery of about 2000 years ago onward.
Met by Dias in 1488. Dutch records name the Goringhaiqua, Cochoqua, Hessequa and others.
After the smallpox of 1713 and the loss of land and herds their societies broke up. Many descendants are among the Coloured people of the Cape.
Khoekhoe herders along the Orange River.
Dutch parties reached Namaqualand in the 1680s. Nama is the one Khoekhoe language still widely spoken.
Hunters and smiths of central Namibia who speak Khoekhoe. Their earlier history is unknown.
Foragers of the whole south, known from stone tools and rock art. Older books say Bushmen.
Pressed into the drier west as farmers and then colonists took the rest.
Foragers of the north-western Kalahari, there for thousands of years by the evidence of archaeology.
The name means true people and is also written Ju/'hoansi. Older books say !Kung.
Foragers of the central Kalahari before travellers wrote of them. Also written G/ui and G//ana.
Foragers of the central Kalahari. Called San, though their languages are Khoe.
Foragers near Lake Eyasi. Their long presence is assumed, not recorded.
Hadzabe. First described by German travellers. About a thousand people.
Their click language may be distantly related to Khoe. Their long presence is assumed.
Farmers and herders today, in the Kondoa hills.
Founded by the Dutch East India Company as a supply station.
Trekking farmers carried its frontier to the Fish and Orange rivers.
British from 1806.
Boer republic north of the Vaal, also called the Transvaal. Britain annexed it after the war of 1899 to 1902.
Boer republic between the Orange and the Vaal.
Founded by freed people from the United States, who settled from 1822. Independent since 1847.
Conquered for Muhammad Ali of Egypt from 1821, with a capital at Khartoum.
Founded by Muhammad Ahmad, the Mahdi. It fell to an Anglo-Egyptian army at Omdurman in 1898.
Ruled jointly in name by Britain and Egypt.
A federation of eight colonies governed from Dakar.
Gabon, Middle Congo, Ubangi-Shari and Chad, governed from Brazzaville.
Northern and southern protectorates, joined in 1914. The Gold Coast, Sierra Leone and the Gambia were the other British colonies in the west.
The private domain of Leopold II until 1908, then a Belgian colony.
Luanda, founded in 1575, and a strip inland along the Kwanza.
The whole territory was occupied only by about 1920.
Forts at Sofala and Mozambique Island and estates along the Zambezi.
Much of it was run by chartered companies until the 1930s.
Tanganyika, Rwanda and Burundi. Divided between Britain and Belgium after 1919.
Kenya and Uganda, and Tanganyika as a mandate after 1919.
Taken by South African forces in 1915 and ruled by South Africa until 1990.
The British South Africa Company's territories on both sides of the Zambezi, with Nyasaland beside them.
The Cape, Natal and the two former Boer republics under white minority rule.
Never colonised, though Italy occupied it from 1936 to 1941. Eritrea separated in 1993.
Independent since 1960. The most populous state in Africa.
Named for the medieval empire. Control of the north has been contested by Tuareg and other armed movements since 2012.
Independent since 1960.
Independent since 1960.
Independent since 1956. The south left in 2011. Civil war since 2023 has divided control of the country.
Independent since 2011. The Abyei area on its northern border is disputed with Sudan.
Formed in 1960 from the Italian and British territories. Somaliland in the north-west declared independence in 1991 and governs itself. Its sovereignty is disputed and is not settled here.
Independent since 1963.
Tanganyika, independent in 1961, united with Zanzibar in 1964.
Independent since 1960. Called Zaire from 1971 to 1997.
Independent since 1975, after a war that began in 1961.
Independent since 1975.
A republic since 1961. Minority rule ended with the election of 1994. It has eleven official spoken languages.
The Irrawaddy valley, where Pyu is written in inscriptions from about the 5th century and died out after the 12th. Earlier placement rests on the Pyu walled towns.
Burmese speakers came down into the dry zone in the 9th century, by most accounts from the Nanzhao borderlands.
The Irrawaddy valley. Burmese is written from the early 12th century, as on the four-language Myazedi inscription.
Arakan, where the Rakhine speak an old-fashioned Burmese. The date of their arrival is uncertain.
The delta and Pegu. Burmese replaced Mon here after the conquests of the 16th century and of 1757.
Tenasserim coast, where Tavoyan is an early offshoot of Burmese. Thinly peopled.
The western hills, thinly peopled. Chin languages are recorded from the 19th century and their earlier presence is inferred.
The far north, thinly peopled. Jingpho (Kachin), Lisu, Rawang and Naga languages are recorded from the 18th and 19th centuries.
Arakan before Burmese. Its early kings wrote Sanskrit and the speech of the people is unknown, so this is a guess.
The hills between the Sittaung and the Salween. When Karen speakers arrived is unknown, and clear records begin in the 18th century.
Karen villages of the Irrawaddy delta.
The Shan plateau, settled by Tai speakers in the 12th and 13th centuries.
Tai speakers of the upper Irrawaddy and Hkamti.
Lower Burma. Mon is written from about the 6th century, and its earlier spread is inferred.
Tenasserim coast. Thinly peopled, and Mon is assumed.
The Chao Phraya plain, the country of Dvaravati, where Old Mon inscriptions are found from the 6th century.
The Khorat plateau, where Mon inscriptions and Buddhist boundary stones are found.
Haripunjaya at Lamphun, a Mon kingdom until 1292.
After the conquest of 1757 most Mon took up Burmese. Mon is still spoken around Mawlamyine.
The lower Mekong. Khmer is assumed for Funan from later inscriptions.
Old Khmer is written from the early 7th century and Khmer has been spoken here ever since.
The Mekong delta, Khmer until Vietnamese settlement in the 17th and 18th centuries.
The Khmer Krom of the lower delta.
The Mun valley and southern Khorat under Chenla and Angkor.
Northern Khmer, still spoken around Surin.
Northern Thailand and Laos before the Tai, thinly peopled. Khmuic and Palaungic languages are assumed from where their speakers live today.
The Shan plateau before the Shan. Palaung and Wa are assumed.
The Khorat plateau before the first Mon and Khmer inscriptions. Which Austroasiatic languages were spoken is unknown.
The middle Mekong before the Lao.
The Annamite range and the central highlands, home of Katuic and Bahnaric languages.
Khmu and related languages in the hills of northern Laos.
Wa and Palaung hills.
Tày and Nùng of the Guangxi border, the southern edge of the old Tai homeland.
Tai of the Black River valleys. The date of their spread is inferred from language and is debated.
Northern Thai, Lue and Lao of the upper Mekong and Ping.
Thai of the Chao Phraya plain, written from the Sukhothai inscriptions of about 1300.
Lao of the middle Mekong and the Khorat plateau.
Southern Thai of the peninsula.
The Red River delta, a Chinese province for most of these years. The people's speech was the ancestor of Vietnamese.
The Red River delta.
The Ma and Ca river plains, the southern part of the old Viet country.
Land ceded by Champa in 1069 and 1306.
Settled after the fall of the Cham capital Vijaya in 1471.
The southern Cham coast, taken between 1611 and 1693.
The Mekong delta. Vietnamese rule at Saigon dates from 1698.
The central highlands, where lowland settlers became the majority in the later 20th century.
The northern Cham coast. Austronesian speakers settled here some centuries before 1 CE, and Cham is written from about the 4th century.
The central Cham coast.
Panduranga, the last Cham country.
Cham is still spoken around Phan Rang, and by Cham communities in Cambodia.
Jarai, Rade and other Chamic languages of the highlands. When Chamic speakers moved inland is unknown.
Hmong and Mien villages on the high ridges of northern Vietnam, Laos and Thailand, settled from China from about 1800.
The peninsula before Malay became general, a thinly peopled forest. Austronesian traders were probably already on the coasts.
The isthmus, thinly peopled. Its languages are unknown, and Aslian and Mon are both possible.
The southern peninsula. Thinly peopled, and the languages are assumed.
The forested interior, where the Orang Asli still speak Aslian languages.
Eastern and southern Sumatra. Inferred from later inscriptions and from comparison of the Malayic languages.
Old Malay is first written at Palembang in 683, on the Kedukan Bukit stone. The circle takes in Minangkabau and the other Malayic languages of Sumatra.
The Riau, Lingga and Natuna islands, home of the sea people, the Orang Laut. Thinly peopled.
The peninsula, which Ptolemy calls the Golden Chersonese. When Malay became its main language is debated.
The peninsula under Malacca and its successor states.
The isthmus under Tambralinga. Its language is uncertain, and Malay and Mon are both likely.
Western Borneo, often proposed as the first home of the Malayic languages. The circle takes in Iban and Kendayan.
Brunei and the north coast.
Banjar Malay of the south-east.
Kutai Malay of the east coast.
Ambon Malay, one of the trade Malays of the eastern islands. Indonesian, the national language, grew from this trade language.
The northern highlands around Lake Toba. Inferred before the first outside reports of the 13th to 16th centuries.
Nias, Mentawai and Enggano, the islands off the west coast. Thinly peopled.
The northern tip before Acehnese. The languages are assumed to have been related to Gayo and Batak.
Acehnese is a Chamic language, close kin of Cham in Vietnam. Linguists put its arrival in Sumatra between the 8th and the 10th century, and the first sure outside record is of 1292.
Western Java. Inferred before the first Old Sundanese inscriptions of the 14th century.
Western Java. Jakarta on the north coast speaks Betawi Malay and Indonesian.
Central Java. Inferred before the first dated Old Javanese inscription of 804.
Central Java, with a written tradition unbroken since the 9th century.
Eastern Java.
Eastern Java, seat of the court from 929.
Madura. Inferred for the early centuries.
Madurese settlers in the eastern salient of Java.
Bali. Inferred before the first Old Balinese inscriptions of the late 9th century.
Bali.
Sasak of Lombok, a close relative of Balinese.
The thinly peopled forest of western and central Borneo. Land Dayak, Kayan and Kenyah languages are known from records only since the 19th century.
The eastern interior. Thinly peopled.
The Barito basin. Ma'anyan, spoken here, is the closest relative of Malagasy.
Dusun, Murut and other languages of Sabah.
Northern Luzon. Inferred before Spanish records.
Ilocano on the coast, Ibanag in the Cagayan valley, and Ifugao, Bontoc and Kankanaey in the mountains.
Ivatan of the Batanes islands.
Central and southern Luzon. Inferred.
A copperplate of 900 found by Laguna de Bay names local places and people, but it is written in Old Malay, so the speech of the country is still inferred.
Spanish friars wrote Tagalog down from the 1570s. It is the base of Filipino, the national language.
The central islands. Inferred before 1521.
Cebuano, Hiligaynon and Waray. Pigafetta took down a Cebuano word list in 1521.
Maguindanao, Maranao, Manobo and other languages of Mindanao, joined by Cebuano settlers in the 20th century.
Tausug and Sama of the Sulu islands.
Palawan and the Calamian islands. Thinly peopled.
Minahasan, Sangir and Mongondow, languages of Philippine type in northern Sulawesi.
The whole island. Taiwan is the oldest home of the Austronesian family, and nine of its ten branches are found only here.
Dutch missionaries wrote Siraya and Favorlang on the western plain in the 17th century.
The mountains and the east coast: Atayal, Bunun, Paiwan, Amis and others. The plains languages gave way to Chinese.
Settlers from Fujian on the south-western plain, under Dutch and then Zheng rule.
The western plain filled with Hokkien and Hakka settlers under Qing rule.
The Taipei basin and, from the 1790s, the Yilan plain.
By 1900 the plains spoke Hokkien and Hakka. Mandarin spread through schools after 1945.
Singapore, mostly Chinese since the 1830s. English is now its common language.
Penang. Chinese and Indian communities live in every town of the peninsula.
South and central Sulawesi. Bugis and Makassar are written in their own script from about the 16th century, and earlier placement is inferred.
Kaili, Pamona, Gorontalo and the languages of the northern and eastern arms.
Tolaki, Muna and Buton in the south-east.
Sumbawa and Bima. Austronesian languages of the eastern islands, shown here in the colour of western Indonesia for want of a closer family.
Manggarai, Ngada, Sikka and the languages of Sumba.
Tetum, Dawan and Rotinese of Timor and Roti.
Seram, Ambon and Buru. Austronesian languages of the central Moluccas, known from records only since the 16th century.
The Sula and Banggai islands.
Austronesian languages of southern Halmahera and the islands around it.
Ternate, Tidore, Galela and Tobelo of northern Halmahera. These languages are not Austronesian and are older on this ground.
Alor, Pantar and eastern Timor: Bunak, Makasae, Fataluku and their relatives.
Bilua, Touo, Lavukaleve and Savosavo, four languages of the central Solomons left from before the Austronesian arrival.
Some seventy Oceanic languages of the Solomon Islands. Pijin, an English-based creole, is now the common language.
Vanuatu, settled by Lapita people about 1000 BCE, has more than a hundred languages. Bislama is the common language today.
Santa Cruz, the Reef Islands and Vanikoro in the outer Solomons, reached by Lapita people about 3,000 years ago.
New Caledonia and the Loyalty Islands, settled by Lapita people about 1000 BCE. Some twenty-eight languages, among them Drehu, Nengone and Paicî.
Fiji was settled by Lapita people about 1000 to 900 BCE. Its languages are the nearest relatives of Polynesian.
Fijian, called Vosa Vakaviti by its speakers, written by missionaries from the 1830s in the dialect of Bau.
Spoken by descendants of labourers brought from India between 1879 and 1916, mostly in the cane districts of the two main islands.
New Caledonia, a French possession since 1853 with a large settler population around Nouméa.
Tahiti, where French is now the usual home language beside Tahitian.
The Marianas were settled about 1500 BCE straight from island Asia. Chamorro, written from 1668, is not Oceanic and its nearest kin lie in the Philippines and Indonesia.
Palau, settled about 1000 BCE or earlier. Palauan also came directly from island Asia.
Yapese, Chuukese, Pohnpeian and Kosraean of the Caroline Islands. The high islands were settled about 2,000 years ago and the dates are debated.
Marshallese. The atolls were settled about 2,000 years ago.
Gilbertese of Kiribati, and Nauruan. The Line Islands far to the east had no settled people when Europeans arrived.
Yap, which the wide Caroline circle does not reach. Yapese stands apart from its neighbours within Oceanic.
Kosrae, settled about 2,000 to 1,800 years ago.
Kiritimati, Tabuaeran and Teraina in the Line Islands, settled by Gilbertese workers and families under colonial rule.
Samoa, settled about 800 BCE. In 1 CE the speech of Samoa and Tonga was still close to the common ancestor of all Polynesian languages.
Samoan.
Tonga, settled about 900 to 850 BCE, the earliest dated landfall in Polynesia.
Tongan. Cook's officers took down the first word lists in the 1770s.
Niue. The date of first settlement is uncertain.
The Society Islands, settled about 1000 to 1100 by radiocarbon dating. Older estimates were centuries earlier, and the dates are debated.
The southern Cook Islands, settled about 1000 to 1100.
The Marquesas, settled about 1100 on current dating.
The Tuamotu atolls. Thinly peopled.
Hawaii was settled from central eastern Polynesia about 1000 to 1200. Radiocarbon dates, language and chiefly genealogies are the evidence, and the date is debated.
ʻŌlelo Hawaiʻi, written from the 1820s and the language of the kingdom. It was banned from schools in 1896.
Niʻihau kept Hawaiian as its daily language. Since the 1980s it has been taught again across the islands.
Easter Island, settled about 1200 on current radiocarbon dating and first visited by Europeans in 1722. Spanish is now widely spoken beside Rapa Nui.
The North Island, Te Ika-a-Māui, settled about 1250 to 1300. Radiocarbon dates, a dated volcanic ash layer and canoe traditions agree closely.
The North Island. Written from the 1810s.
The South Island, Te Waipounamu. Thinly peopled, with most people on the east and north coasts.
The East Coast, Bay of Plenty and Urewera, where Māori stayed the community language longest. It is an official language and widely taught.
Northland.
The North Island. Settlers outnumbered Māori from about 1858.
The South Island, settled from the 1840s and quickly by gold seekers after 1861.
Hawaii. English and Hawaiian Pidgin became general among plantation workers from Asia, Portugal and the islands.
The north, first settled about 500 to 700 along the coasts, though traces of earlier visitors are disputed. Malagasy is a Barito language from Borneo with Bantu, Malay and Javanese loanwords.
The south and the highlands, thinly peopled in the first centuries.
The north. Malagasy is also spoken by a minority on Mayotte.
The south and the highlands.
The north. Written in Arabic script in the south-east before 1600 and in Latin script from the 1820s.
The south and the highlands.
The Comoros were settled about 700 to 900. Comorian is a Bantu language close to Swahili.
Réunion had no people before French settlement in 1665. Its creole grew among settlers and enslaved people from Madagascar, Africa and India.
Mauritius had no people before a Dutch post of 1638 to 1710, and lasting settlement began under France in 1721. Bhojpuri, French and English are also used.
Rodrigues, settled from the 1790s.
A trading kingdom of the Mekong delta known by its Chinese name, with its main sites at Oc Eo and Angkor Borei. Its language was probably Khmer.
Khmer kingdoms of the middle Mekong that absorbed Funan, known by their Chinese name. The first inscriptions in Old Khmer are theirs.
Jayavarman II was consecrated universal king in 802, as a later inscription tells.
At its widest, from the Mekong delta to the Chao Phraya plain and the Khorat plateau. Angkor Wat was built in the 12th century.
Zhou Daguan saw Angkor in 1296. The court left it after Ayutthaya's attack of 1431.
The Khmer kingdom after Angkor, with capitals at Longvek and Oudong, squeezed between Siam and Vietnam. A French protectorate from 1863.
Mon Buddhist towns of the Chao Phraya plain, taking shape in the later 6th century. Known from archaeology before the name appears.
The name is found on silver medals from Nakhon Pathom and in Chinese accounts of the 7th century. The towns passed under Khmer power in the 11th century.
A Mon kingdom at Lamphun. Its founding by Queen Camadevi is chronicle tradition, and its own Mon inscriptions date from the 12th century.
The Mon country of Lower Burma, with towns at Thaton and Pegu. The chronicle story of a great kingdom of Thaton taken by Pagan in 1057 is doubted by some scholars.
The Mon kingdom of Lower Burma, rich from sea trade, conquered by Toungoo in 1539.
Restored for seventeen years and destroyed by Alaungpaya in 1757.
After 1757 many Mon fled to Siam and most of the rest took up Burmese. Mon State lies around Mawlamyine.
Walled brick towns at Beikthano, Halin and Sri Ksetra, known from archaeology.
Pyu inscriptions and Tang accounts of the Piao kingdom. Nanzhao sacked Halin in 832.
The chronicles date the walls of Pagan to 849. Little is certain before Anawrahta.
The first Burmese kingdom to rule the whole Irrawaddy valley. Mongol invasion ended it in 1287.
The Burmese kingdom of the dry zone after Pagan, at war with Pegu and the Shan states.
A small Burmese kingdom on the Sittaung that took Pegu in 1539.
Under Bayinnaung it held Lan Na, the Shan states, and for a time Ayutthaya and Lan Xang.
Restored at Ava and smaller. It fell to the revived Mon kingdom in 1752.
Founded by Alaungpaya. It conquered the Mon, Arakan and Manipur and sacked Ayutthaya in 1767.
It lost the coasts to Britain in 1826 and 1852 and the rest in 1885.
A Rakhine kingdom on the Bay of Bengal, tied by trade to Bengal and to the Portuguese. Burma conquered it in 1785.
The people of the Red River delta under the Chinese provinces of Jiaozhi and later Annan. The Dong Son bronze culture was theirs, and the Trưng sisters led a rising in 40.
Independent after Ngô Quyền's victory of 938, and named Đại Việt from 1054. It beat back Mongol and Ming armies.
Lê Thánh Tông took the Cham capital in 1471 and settlers moved south.
The north of divided Vietnam, ruled by the Trịnh lords in the name of the Lê kings. Europeans called it Tonkin.
The south under the Nguyễn lords at Huế, known to Europeans as Cochinchina.
The Nguyễn took the last Cham lands and settled the Mekong delta. The Tây Sơn rising overthrew them in 1777.
Gia Long united the country in 1802 and named it Việt Nam.
The capital at Huế. France took the south in the 1860s and made the rest a protectorate by 1884.
The southern provinces around Gia Định, now Ho Chi Minh City.
An Iron Age culture of jar burials on the central coast, tied by trade to the Philippines and Taiwan. Most scholars see its people as ancestors of the Cham.
Chinese histories date the kingdom they call Linyi from 192. Cham inscriptions begin about the 4th century at Mỹ Sơn.
Kauthara and Panduranga in the south. The Võ Cạnh stone near Nha Trang is the oldest Sanskrit inscription of Southeast Asia, dated between the 2nd and 4th centuries.
Panduranga, the last Cham principality, annexed by Vietnam in 1832.
The Cham of Ninh Thuận and Bình Thuận. A larger number, mostly Muslim, live along the Mekong in Cambodia.
Karen speakers were probably in these hills long before the first clear records. Pagan inscriptions of the 13th century may name them, and that reading is not certain.
Karen is the outside name, and the Sgaw call themselves Pgaz K'Nyau. Missionaries and British officers described them from the early 19th century.
The peoples of the western hills before outside records. Their presence is inferred from their languages.
Chin is the Burmese name, and Zo, Lai and Asho are among their own names. Recorded by British officers in the 19th century.
The Jingpho and their neighbours spread south through these hills in recent centuries. Before British records this is inferred.
Kachin is the outside name for the Jingpho and their neighbours, recorded by British officers from the 1820s and 1830s.
Hmong families moved from southern China onto the high ridges of Vietnam and Laos between about 1790 and the 1860s. Their own tradition and later accounts are the evidence for the first decades.
Recorded by French officers and in colonial counts from the later 19th century. Miao and Meo are outside names.
Peoples of the central highlands of Vietnam, whom French writers called Montagnards. Jarai and Rade speak Chamic languages and Bahnar an Austroasiatic one.
Semai, Temiar, Jahai and other forest peoples of the peninsula, known from archaeology and language before the 19th century. Orang Asli, original people, is the modern Malay term.
Tai speakers of the hills north of the Red River delta, kin of the Zhuang across the border. Named in Vietnamese annals from the 11th century.
Small Tai principalities under hereditary lords, tributary to Burma for most of their history until the lords gave up their powers in 1959. The Shan call themselves Tai Yai.
The first large Thai kingdom, founded on a Khmer outpost. The founding date of 1238 is conventional and rests on later reckoning.
The inscription credited to King Ram Khamhaeng is dated 1292, and some doubt its age. Ayutthaya made Sukhothai a province in 1438.
Founded by Mangrai, who took Mon Haripunjaya and built Chiang Mai in 1296.
Under Burma from 1558 and tributary to Siam from 1775, until Bangkok took direct control.
The Lao kingdom of the middle Mekong, founded by Fa Ngum at Luang Prabang.
Luang Prabang, one of the three kingdoms Lan Xang split into.
Vientiane, destroyed by Siam in 1828.
Champasak in the south.
Founded in 1351 on the lower Chao Phraya. It absorbed Sukhothai and broke Angkor.
A great trading capital known to foreigners as Siam. Burmese armies destroyed it in 1767.
Restored at Thonburi and then Bangkok, with Lao, Khmer and Malay tributaries.
Siam gave up its Lao, Khmer and Malay dependencies to France and Britain and kept its independence. Renamed Thailand in 1939.
A port at the Bujang valley on the crossing to the east coast. A Chola inscription names it as Kadaram, raided in 1025, and its language is assumed.
Founded at Palembang. Yijing stayed here in 671, and the Kedukan Bukit stone of 683 records its king's expedition.
Master of both shores of the straits and of the trade between India and China. A Chola fleet raided its ports in 1025.
The Chinese go on naming Sanfoqi, by now centred at Jambi.
The kingdom of the Batang Hari, heir to Srivijaya. Its king Adityawarman moved inland to the Minangkabau highlands about 1347.
A kingdom of the isthmus at Nakhon Si Thammarat, named in Chola and Chinese sources. Its language is uncertain, and it passed to the Thai in the late 13th century.
The first Muslim sultanate of the islands. The founding date of 1267 comes from later tradition.
Marco Polo stopped here in 1292 and Ibn Battuta in the 1340s. The name Sumatra comes from Samudra.
Founded about 1400 by a prince from Palembang and taken by the Portuguese in 1511. Its court set the pattern of Malay language, law and Islam.
Founded by the heirs of Malacca, with the Riau islands. Divided between British and Dutch spheres in 1824.
A Malay port founded, by its own chronicle, about the middle of the 15th century. The date is not secure.
A Malay sultanate and pepper port, often tributary to Siam, which conquered it in 1785 and 1786. Its people still speak Malay.
The strongest Muslim state of the straits in the 16th and 17th centuries. It fought the Dutch from 1873 to 1903.
Chinese histories record envoys from Boni from 977. Most scholars place it at or near Brunei.
A Muslim sultanate that held the north coast of Borneo. Pigafetta described its court in 1521.
Reduced step by step by Sulu, Sarawak and North Borneo. Under British protection from 1888.

Seven stone posts with Sanskrit inscriptions of King Mulawarman, from about 400, the oldest writing in Indonesia. They do not name the kingdom, which is called after the district, and the language of his people is assumed.
A Malay-speaking sultanate at Banjarmasin, founded by its own tradition in 1526.
Grown rich on pepper and known to the Dutch from the early 17th century. The Dutch abolished it in 1860.
A pottery-making culture of the north coast of western Java, with Indian trade goods. Known only from archaeology.
Sanskrit inscriptions of King Purnavarman near Jakarta and Bogor, from about 450. The speech of his people is assumed to be early Sundanese.
Central Java from the Canggal inscription of 732. The Buddhist Sailendras built Borobudur about 800 and their Shaivite rivals Prambanan.
The court moved to eastern Java under Mpu Sindok in 929. The kingdom is also called Medang.
Airlangga restored the eastern Javanese kingdom from 1019, and Kediri followed it from 1045. A great age of Old Javanese poetry.
Founded by Ken Angrok. Its last king Kertanagara sent an expedition to Sumatra and defied Kublai Khan.
Founded in 1293 after a Mongol fleet was driven off.
Its height under Hayam Wuruk and Gajah Mada. The Nagarakretagama claims dependencies from Sumatra to New Guinea, and how real that rule was is debated.
Weakened by civil war and the rise of the Muslim ports.
The Hindu kingdom of western Java, with its capital at Pakuan near Bogor. Banten ended it in 1579.
The first Muslim state of Java, a port on the north coast. Its beginnings are obscure and the date of 1475 is traditional.
Described by Pires about 1515. It brought down the last of Majapahit in 1527.
A pepper sultanate at the western tip of Java, ruling Lampung across the strait. Under Dutch control from 1682.
Under Sultan Agung it ruled most of Java and attacked Batavia in 1628 and 1629.
The two courts Mataram was divided into in 1755. Yogyakarta's sultan still governs its special region.
The Warmadewa kings, known from inscriptions beginning with the Belanjong pillar of 914.
Conquered by Majapahit in 1343. Gelgel, Klungkung and other courts kept Hindu Javanese culture alive until the Dutch conquest of 1906 to 1908.
A copperplate of 900 found by Laguna de Bay, written in Old Malay with Sanskrit and Old Javanese words, names Tondo and its chief.
No local writing survives from these centuries. Trade goods and brief Chinese notices of Luzon are the evidence.
Pires wrote of Luzon traders at Malacca about 1515. By 1570 Maynila was ruled by Muslim kin of the sultans of Brunei, and Spain took it in 1571.
A gold-trading port of northern Mindanao that sent envoys to Song China from 1001.
Large plank boats and gold work have been dug up here. No record names the port again until Magellan's men met its ruler in 1521.
A Visayan port whose earlier history rests on legend written down much later, with no dates.
Under Rajah Humabon when Magellan arrived in 1521. Legazpi took it for Spain in 1565.
A Tausug sultanate at Jolo. Most historians date its founding to about 1457 and one tradition to 1405.
Strong at sea in the 18th century. Its old claim to eastern Sabah is still disputed between the Philippines and Malaysia.
Zainal Abidin, by tradition the first ruler to take the title of sultan, reigned from 1486. Tradition written down later puts the first king in 1257, and nothing written at the time survives.
A clove island whose sultans claimed islands from Sulawesi to the Papuan coast, described by the Portuguese from 1512. Its language is Papuan, and Tidore across the strait was its twin and rival.
A Dutch vassal from 1683.
The twin kingdom of Gowa and Tallo. Muslim from 1605, it made Makassar the great free port of the east until the Dutch took it in 1669.
The Austronesian peoples of the whole island, known before 1600 from archaeology and from the depth of their languages.
Dutch records name the Siraya and other plains peoples and the kingdom of Middag.
Atayal, Amis, Paiwan, Bunun, Truku and others of the mountains and the east. Sixteen peoples are officially recognised.
Ifugao, Bontoc, Kankanaey, Kalinga and others of the Cordillera, never brought under Spanish rule. Igorot is a lowland word for mountain people, and many prefer their own names.
The people of Manila Bay and the lakes south of it, who used their own script, baybayin, when Spain arrived.
Song writers describe raiders called Pisheye, whom many take to be Visayans. The link is not certain.
The peoples of the central islands. Spaniards called the tattooed Visayans Pintados.
Islam reached Sulu in the 14th century and Mindanao about 1500, by the peoples' own genealogies, which were written down later.

Maguindanao, Maranao, Tausug, Sama and other Muslim peoples of Mindanao and Sulu, with the sultanate of Maguindanao strongest in the 17th century. Moro was the Spanish name and is now used with pride, as in Bangsamoro.
The inland peoples of Borneo, known from archaeology and language. The ancestors of the Malagasy sailed from the south-east of this island.
Iban, Bidayuh, Kayan, Kenyah, Ngaju and many others. Dayak is a collective name used by outsiders and now by the peoples themselves.
Highland peoples around Lake Toba, perhaps the Bata of a 13th century Chinese list.
Toba, Karo, Simalungun, Mandailing and others, with their own script. Named by Pires about 1515.
The people of the western highlands, with the inland kingdom of Pagaruyung from the 14th century. Known for descent through mothers and for wide migration.
The kingdoms of Luwu, Bone and Wajo, remembered in the La Galigo epic and in chronicles written later.
Bone led the Bugis after 1669. Bugis traders and settlers spread from the Malay peninsula to northern Australia.
The Tetun of central Timor and their ritual centre at Wehali, which many Timorese domains acknowledged. Pigafetta heard of Timor's kings in 1522.
The people of the Mariana Islands, settled between about 1500 and 1100 BCE in one of the longest open-sea crossings of its time. Their stone house pillars, latte, date from about 900.
Magellan landed at Guam in 1521. Spanish conquest after 1668 and disease cut their numbers by nine tenths or more.
Settled about 1000 BCE or earlier and first described in writing in 1783. Great earth terraces were built in the first millennium.
The people of Chuuk and the atolls, settled about 2,000 years ago. Their navigators kept the art of star-path sailing alive into the present.
The Saudeleur rulers of Pohnpei built Nan Madol, a town of basalt islets on the reef. Tradition tells of their overthrow, which is dated by counting generations.
Atoll dwellers of two island chains, settled about 2,000 years ago, who mapped swells with stick charts.
The people of the Gilbert Islands. Settlement about 2,000 years ago is inferred, and tradition tells of later arrivals from Samoa.
The main islands have been peopled for some 30,000 years. Oceanic speakers arrived about 3,000 years ago and a few Papuan languages survive beside them.
Mendaña's Spanish ships reached Santa Isabel and Guadalcanal in 1568. The peoples of Malaita, Guadalcanal, New Georgia and the other islands keep their own names.
Settled by Lapita people about 1000 BCE. Tradition tells of the chief Roy Mata, and his burial with his followers was found where the story placed it.
Quirós landed on Espiritu Santo in 1606 and Cook charted the group in 1774 as the New Hebrides.
The people of New Caledonia, settled by Lapita people about 1000 BCE. The Lapita site that names the culture is on this island.

Cook landed in 1774 and France annexed the island in 1853. Kanak is the name the people chose for themselves in the 20th century, and the future status of New Caledonia is contested and not settled here.
Fiji was settled about 1000 to 900 BCE and stayed in touch with Tonga and Samoa. Hill forts multiplied after about 1200.
iTaukei, the owners of the land, is the official name for indigenous Fijians. The chiefdom of Bau led the islands before cession to Britain in 1874.
Tonga was settled about 900 to 850 BCE. Here and in Samoa the Lapita settlers became the first Polynesians.
Cook visited three times in the 1770s. Tonga was united under George Tupou I in 1845.
Samoa was settled about 800 BCE. Its chiefly titles and genealogies reach back many centuries, with dates counted from generations.
Sighted by Roggeveen in 1722. Missionaries arrived in 1830.

The sacred kings of Tonga drew tribute, stone and marriage partners from Samoa, eastern Fiji and islands beyond, an influence wider than this circle. Tradition traces the line to about 950, and their stone-faced tombs date from about 1300.
The people of the Society Islands, settled about 1000 to 1100. Ra'iatea and its temple Taputapuātea were a religious centre for islands far away.
Wallis reached Tahiti in 1767 and Cook in 1769. Tahitian is the outside name.
The people of the Marquesas, who say ʻEnana and Te Henua ʻEnana in the north and ʻEnata and Te Fenua ʻEnata in the south. Dates for first settlement run from the 10th to the late 12th century.
Mendaña named the islands in 1595. Disease in the 19th century left only a few thousand survivors.
The people of Rarotonga, Aitutaki and their neighbours, settled about 1000 to 1100. Tradition makes Rarotonga a starting point of canoes for Aotearoa.
Settled from central eastern Polynesia about 1000 to 1200. By 1700 the islands held large chiefdoms with irrigated fields and fishponds.
Cook arrived in 1778. Hawaiian is the outside name.
The people of Easter Island, settled about 1200. They carved and raised nearly a thousand stone figures, the moai.
Roggeveen landed in 1722. Slave raids from Peru in 1862 and disease left barely a hundred people on the island, which is now part of Chile.
Aotearoa was settled about 1250 to 1300 from central eastern Polynesia, and iwi trace descent from the founding canoes. The Moriori of the Chatham Islands are a related people too far east to draw.
Te Waipounamu, the South Island, home of Waitaha, Ngāti Māmoe and Ngāi Tahu. Thinly peopled, as crops grew poorly this far south.
Tasman sighted the coast in 1642 and Cook circled it in 1769. The Treaty of Waitangi was signed in 1840.
Ngāi Tahu of the South Island.
Settlers from Borneo and from the African coast, on the coasts first and in the highlands by about 1200. Tradition calls the earliest highland people Vazimba, and the dates are debated.
A people of the south-east coast whose scribes wrote Malagasy in Arabic script, in manuscripts called sorabe.
The people of the central highlands around Antananarivo, whose royal traditions were written down in the 19th century. Europeans called them Hova, properly the name of one rank.
The Sakalava kingdom of Menabe was founded on the west coast by Andriandahifotsy in the 17th century. Its early dates come from royal tradition and differ between accounts.
Cattle-keeping kingdoms of the west coast, Menabe and from about 1690 Boina, the strongest power on the island in the 18th century.
The many inseparables, a league of east coast peoples joined by Ratsimilaho about 1712.

Bantu-speaking islanders with Arab, Persian and Malagasy ties, whose oldest known villages date from the 8th to 10th centuries. Sovereignty over Mayotte is disputed today between the Comoros and France.
Spain held Cebu from 1565 and Manila from 1571. Its rule never reached the Cordillera or most of Mindanao and Sulu.
Taken from Spain in 1898 and held after a war against the Philippine Republic. Independent in 1946.
The Dutch East India Company at Batavia from 1619, with forts in Maluku, Makassar and the north coast of Java.
The Dutch state took over in 1800 and reached its full extent only about 1910. Japan occupied it from 1942 to 1945.
Cochinchina, Annam, Tonkin and Cambodia joined in 1887, and Laos in 1893.
Arakan and Tenasserim from 1826 and Pegu from 1852.
All of Burma, governed as a province of India until 1937.
The Straits Settlements of Penang, Malacca and Singapore from 1826, and protected Malay states from 1874.
Sarawak under the Brooke rajahs from 1841 and North Borneo under a chartered company from 1881.
A Dutch company colony on the south-west coast, driven out by Zheng Chenggong in 1662.
The Zheng family kingdom of Tungning ruled the west coast from 1662. The Qing took it in 1683 and governed the plains but not the mountains.
Ceded to Japan in 1895 and ruled by it until 1945.
Governed since 1945 by the Republic of China. Its status is disputed and this atlas does not settle it.
Kamehameha I united the islands between 1795 and 1810. The monarchy was overthrown in 1893 and the United States annexed the islands in 1898.
A kingdom since 1845, with a constitution of 1875. A British protected state from 1900 to 1970, it was never colonised.
Andrianampoinimerina united the highlands from about 1787.
Recognised by Britain as the Kingdom of Madagascar in 1817, it came to rule about two thirds of the island. France conquered it in 1895 and ended the monarchy in 1897.
A French colony until independence in 1960.
Independent as Burma in 1948 and renamed Myanmar in 1989. Armed conflict between the central state and minority peoples has lasted since independence.
Siam took the name Thailand in 1939.
Independent from France in 1953.
Independent from France in 1953.
Independence was declared in 1945. The country was divided into north and south from 1954 until 1975 and formally reunited in 1976.
Malaya became independent in 1957 and joined with Sarawak and Sabah as Malaysia in 1963.
Sarawak and Sabah, the Borneo states of Malaysia.
Independence was declared in 1945 and recognised in 1949. Indonesian, a form of Malay, is the national language beside some seven hundred others.
A republic since 1946. Filipino and English are official, and the Bangsamoro region in the south has governed itself since 2019.
A British colony from 1874 and independent in 1970. Fijian, English and Fiji Hindi are official.
A British colony from 1840 and self-governing from the 1850s. Māori and English are both official languages.
Independent in 1960. Malagasy and French are official.
